Mr. Speaker, on March 14 I inquired of the Postmaster General (Mr. Sauve) the amount paid each year to Mr. Laurent of Montreal. I was promised that I would have this information last week but so far I have not received it. I should like to know when I will have it.

Mr. Speaker, it was my intention to give this information to the hon. gentleman to-day. On March 14 when the estimates of the Post Office Department were under consideration the hon. member for Temis-couata (Mr. Pouliot) asked for certain details in connection with a temporary contract awarded to Mr. J. E. Laurent for the carrying of parcel post and mail matter in Montreal. At that time I stated that I had not all the details but would furnish all the information to be found in the department as soon as possible, some of the details dating back as far as four years. I have been informed by the officers of my department that before May 1, 1932, the carrying of mail matter between the post office and the Stephens building in Montreal was done exclusively by the department. At that time the department maintained a garage containing eight trucks and one motorcycle. The cost of gasoline, oil, et cetera, amounted to $4,977.06 while $19,920 was paid in salaries.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. The information now being given by the Postmaster General is entirely outside of the question I asked. I wanted to know the amount paid to Mr. Laurent each year and the minister is now making an apology for his dealings in the matter.
Order.
I do not want to waste the time of the house.
I want to give an explanation to the hon. member for Temiscouata, in accordance with his questions.

I would point out that under orders of the day questions are directed to ministers of the government only with respect to matters of policy and so forth. In view of the nature of the question asked by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), I think the answer should be as brief as possible and there should be no argument or debate with respect to the subject matter of the question.

Further costs were: garage,
$4,644; depreciation, $3,454.22; interest on capital invested, $829. The total cost of this service was $33,824.28. By reason of difficulties we met in the control of this service, and also of the abuses we discovered, the department had to dismiss employees and thought it advisable to try a new method, that is, to give this service to a contractor for a trial. The contract was awarded to Mr. J. E. Laurent at $27,000, as I said, including the insurance and all the obligations and responsibilities relating to the service. The new method being a trial, the department has adopted the principle of a temporary agreement, which the previous administration had followed from 1921 to 1930, in regard to the Canadian Transfer Company. Under the present contractor this service, from March 1, 1934, to February 28, 1935, has cost the department $28,593.60. But it is due in part to the fact that the normal increase of the parcel post in Montreal has advanced by about seven per cent These two services cost the department, before Mr. Laurent, $57,220.53.

I rise to a point of order. There are only two official languages, English and French. The minister is now speaking the Esperanto language, and no one has understood a word of what he has said. Therefore he should translate either in plain English or French what he has already said in Esperanto.
Order.

If Mr. Speaker understands
it, and the house, I am satisfied.
It is Esperanto.

Since Mr. Laurent has had
the contract, the services are costing the department $55,593.60. Not only has the service been improved but the rolling stock has also been improved to answer the needs of the postal service. speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, March 22, consideration of the motion of Hon. E. N. Rhodes ^Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
With those on this side of the
house I have listened, as we always listen, with a great deal of pleasure to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) in the presentation of his annual budget

The Budget-Mr. Ralston
speech. We listened this time with perhaps rather more interest, because we realized that the Minister of Finance was playing the leading role in the farewell performance of this government in that annual play of lights and shadows which is called the budget. I wish to congratulate my hon. friend, as I always can, on the way in which he filled the role. He lived up to the best traditions of the high office which he occupies. But I do feel that when the time comes for the authors of the piece-and after all many a good actor is spoiled by the lines he is given-for his collaborators, his colleagues in the government, to come before the curtain, the results in the nine by-elections which have already taken place and in the four provincial elections indicate pretty well the reception which they will get.
My hon. friend's speech was, if I may say so without offence, a bit dreary. I noticed a number of hon. members opposite who succumbed to the arms of Morpheus during its delivery and there may also have been those on this side who did likewise; I do not know. But there was to those of us who sit on this side of the house at least one very interesting feature of the budget, and that was the indication which ran like a red thread through the whole speech that at long last the government had come to realize that the trade and tariff policies which had been nearly the ruination of this country for the past four years had been futile. We were reminded-and I shall compare portions of what my hon. friend said in his budget speech with them1-of some utterances which were made just before the last election and which were couched1 in an entirely different tone from that employed by my hon. friend the other afternoon. I refer to the speech of the Prime Minister at Vancouver when he said:
If Mr. Mackenzie King thinks I will not so build up our agricultural and industrial life that its strength will drive our products into the markets of the world, then he is wrong. For that I will do. If he thinks I will not establish new markets for these products, strive with all my heart to retain them, drive our products with all my power into new markets, into old markets, into reluctant markets, he is wrong. For that I will do.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, bear.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If my hon. friends will applaud-what is the fact-that in the last year the total trade of Canada was just one-half the average trade of the last five years of Liberal rule, they will realize how successful that driving has been. This is another speech
made in Winnipeg when he said addressing the farmers:	.
Tell me, when did free trade fight for you? You say tariffs are only for the manufacturers.
I will make them fight for you as well. I will use them to blast a way into the markets that have been closed to you.
And then at Victoria he said:
It is true we must have foreign markets-

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There are signs of conversion even across the way among my hon. friends.
It is true we must have foreign markets, and as I said the other evening we will blast a way to those markets on a worldwide basis with any exportable surpluses. We do not have to worry about that.
What a change there has been. After these speeches the Prime Minister went to Great Britain in 1932 with his policy of blasting a way into the markets of the world, having made a ten per cent increase in tariffs before he went, and demanded that they must take steps without delay; that there was no room for compromise; that it was a time for plain speaking; that they must decide once and for all, and my right hon. friend with his musket on his shoulder, a machine gun under one arm and an ammonal tube under the other started out to blast a way into the markets of the world. The government put up tariffs; in 1930 they raised the tariff on one hundred and six items; in 1931 on a hundred and twenty-nine items and in 1932 on one hundred and thirty-eight items or a tariff increase on three hundred and seventy-three items altogether. They invented a new form of dumping duty, a provision whereby valuations for duty purposes should be based not on the domestic price of the goods which were being imported but on the cost in this country. That however was not good enough and they changed it next year so that valuations need have no principle, no standard whatever in order to be fixed by the Minister of National Revenue. They put on exchange dumping and they provided for seasonal valuations; they did everything they could to provide for exchange controls and invented every possible device by which the business men and consumers of this country might be irritated. That was all done as a means of blasting a way into the markets of the world. Now, having led the world in that, having taken a place in the vanguard of economic nationalism, because that is what they did, having
The Budget-Mr. Ralston

proclaimed the doctrine of Canada first, they come here in 1935 with the Minister ol Finance giving utterance to these words:
The unsatisfactory conditions in agriculture and certain other primary industries are in the main due to the low level of international trade resulting from the spread throughout the world of exaggerated economic nationalism, excessive interferences with trade through quotas and exchange controls, and fluctuating currencies.
il say that we welcome this budget in that it indicates at least a last-minute repentance, a last-minute change, an admission now that the tariff policies which were laid down in 1930, 1931, and 1932 were wrong.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not at all.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance in the budget speech mentioned in one place :
The obstinate adherence to extreme policies of economic nationalism.
But he is not alone in that; his right hon. leader went to Kingston the other night where he is reported in the Ottawa Journal of February 21 to have said:
With the Aladdin lamp of modern production at their elbow, with large sections of their population in want, tariff barriers are erected, quotas established, exchanges controlled, in an ever-failing effort to restore the productive machine by creating a semblance of scarcity.
With all due respect, to hear this government rebuke economic nationalism sounds extremely like Satan rebuking sin. Could one imagine a more complete turnover than that which is evidenced by the sentiments in the budget speech, by the boasts which are being made, not about blasting our way into the markets of the world, but about reductions in duties and apologies for increases in tariffs on the ground that they are made on the recommendation of the tariff board? That does not sound very much like the government of a few years ago. To-day the order of the hour is to see how many duties can be reduced. Why? In order to curry favour with the people of the Dominion of Canada who realize that the avenues of trade have been blocked for the last four years, resulting in this country being reduced to its present condition. That is one of the things which is interesting in this budget. Then, in order that my hon. friend may indicate how much interested the government has suddenly become in international trade, you will find in the speech reference to negotiations with the United States. The minister boasts of reductions in tariffs. I will undertake to say that very seldom have you found a Tory
Mr. Ralston.]
budget speech boasting about reductions in
tariffs. But on page 1988 you find this:
Reference to the fact that to-day's resolutions add no fewer than twenty important commodities to the free list under the British preferential tariff provides an opportunity to point to the record of this government in that regard.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I wonder if it has anything to do with elections? I wonder if it is part of the reform program? I wonder if it has been induced by the results of the by-elections last September? Have they caused this government to see the error of its ways and to realize that the thing to do is to remove the barriers to trade rather than put up others? It is possible.
I want for a moment to make an examination of one or two items in the tariff to see whether close examination reveals a real change of heart, or whether like other features of the reform program it is mostly on the surface and by way of pious phrases. The woollen schedule has interested the people of Canada for the last two years particularly. The woollen schedule includes goods used by those engaged in the primary industries, by the ordinary citizens of the dominion. The woollen industry has been the subject of representations to the government and to the tariff board. In 1932 I pressed on the government one particular item in the woollen schedule, item 554 of the tariff, as to which I contended that the duty under the British preference was practically 61 per cent on most goods coming under that item. That was an inclusive item which covered clothing and material used in clothing for the ordinary individual in this country. Why do I say that the duty was 60 or 61 per cent? Under the British preference the duty was 27i, per cent ad valorem and added to that was 18J cents per pound specific duty. Taking the cost of the average material under that item used by the average man it worked out at 61 per cent. What do we find under this budget? Three of the forty-seven items on which there is a reduction under the British preference have to do with the woollen schedule. And what is the reduction under the professions made by my hon. friend in respect to his conversion to lower tariffs? The 27J per cent ad valorem still remains

The Budget-Mr. Ralston
on this item, but the specific duty has been reduced, the 18J cents per pound now becomes 17 cents. A reduction of li cents per pound. I made inquiry and I am sure that it does not mean more than 2 per cent reduction, and it may not mean more than 1 per cent. So I think I am correct in saying that in respect to at least some items in this schedule, which is a most important one to the average people of this country, there are shown no very substantial " works meet for repentance." The Minister of Finance took up the time of the house putting these three items in the schedule and calling attention to the reductions which had been made. I call attention to the hollowness of those reductions, when one comes to compare them with the tariffs that existed before.
I find another interesting item; overcoats for fishermen, farmers, miners, lumbermen, get only 1 per cent reduction, but overcoats for tennis balls go on the free list altogether. They had 27J per cent ad valorem against them and 18J cents per pound specific, but now Melton cloth to cover tennis balls has been put on the free list as far as the British preference is concerned. That is the gesture my hon. friend makes to the people of this country on the woollen schedule.
I find another class of articles which have been put on the free list, toy construction sets. I understand that in the course of a year there are perhaps 825,000 to $30,000 worth of those goods coming in; not a very large item. The question has occurred to some on this side of the house: is it possible that this has something to do with the government's relief construction program, that these toy construction sets are to be used in connection with that toy relief bill on which $40,000,000 was voted last year and in connection with which only $8,000,000 has been spent? I submit that taking items like the woollen schedule and toy construction sets and counting them as reductions would rather indicate that this program is very much related to that reform program, and that there is just about as much substance in this reduction of tariffs and about as much relief to the consumer as there is to the aid to be given the taxpayers of the Dominion of Canada by their national economic advisory council that is going to sit twice every year as part of the reform program. Or there is going to be just as much benefit to the consumers of 'Canada from these nominal reductions as there is to the working man who is out of a job to-day by reason of the fact that there is going to be an unemployment insurance act on the statute books whereby provided he has paid contributions for forty weeks he may be able to get some insurance for a few weeks when he is out of work.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that perhaps one might say without offence that this whole program of reform and of tariff reductions takes somewhat the form of a make believe program. It is a sort of "let's pretend" reduction and the budget itself as far as reductions in tariff are concerned could, I think, fairly be classed as a make believe budget.
I notice another item. I notice that slipper cloth is substantially reduced.

speechtext: For the sleepers.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think there will be lots of opportunity for the use of carpet slippers on the part of my hon. friends opposite after the next election, when they may warm their feet by the winter fire instead of coming here. Possibly it may have been self-interest to some extent, not at all corrupt self-interest, which influenced the reduction of that particular item. We on this side of the house submit that that tendency, that feverish anxiety which is suggested in the budget regarding international trade and the confession of the undesirability of economic nationalism, is a belated and ludicrous attempt to make the people of Canada believe that the government have been converted.
Turning now for a moment to the matter of an agreement with the United States, my hon. friend the Minister of Finance took a good deal of space in his budget speech to discuss negotiations with the United States. There was a time when negotiations with the United States were not to be mentioned among Christians, particularly on the opposite side of the house. The right hon. Prime Minister in 1911 is reported in Hansard, 1911, on page 23, as saying:
One of the strongest reasons I had for opposing the reciprocity agreement was that it threw into the melting pot for solution a question that involved a problem of patriotism.
Yet to-day they are engaged in negotiations with that country with the problem of patriotism still before them.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What year was that?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The year 1911. It will be recalled that a gentleman who for many years occupied a front seat on the other side of the house and who unfortunately is gone from us now, said on more than one occasion,
The Budget-Mr. Ralston

and publicly too, that he believed it was a serious thing for the Dominion of Canada when reciprocity was defeated. In 1911 we had my right hon. friend the present leader of the government urging that a problem of patriotism was involved, and that therefore he was against reciprocity. Then 1933 came along, only a year ago. What was the attitude of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance then? Was he keen about an agreement with the United States? This is what he said in his budget speech a year ago:
We can only be ready and willing to avail ourselves of any proposals that are fair and reasonable and not of such character which will involve injury to this country if they are speedily terminated.
At that time I urged my hon. friend to pursue negotiations. We pointed out to him, however, that we were afraid his hands were tied to a considerable extent by the Ottawa agreements, in view of the fact that on 159 items we had agreed to preserve the margin of preference to Great Britain and that therefore the duty had to remain as it was because of the fact that those items were on the free list to Great Britain. Last year my hon. friend was only ready and willing to avail himself of any proposals that were fair and reasonable; now there is the sound of going in the tops of the mulberry trees. Now, according to the budget speech, we are not simply ready and willing to avail ourselves of any proposals; we are the aggressors now; we are the ones who are anxious. The minister said:
These negotiations will be actively prosecuted by the government of Canada, and every possible step is being, and will be taken with the object in mind of effecting a satisfactory trade agreement having for its aim the lowering of trade barriers with consequent increased flow of trade resulting in mutual advantage.
That is very different from the static attitude of last year. I wonder if that has any reference at all to the by-elections of last September, and if that hitches up with the reform program and the reductions in duty which are mentioned in other parts of the budget. That, Mr. Speaker, indicates a complete change of front, and the ubiquitous minister to the United States is burning up axle grease and rails at the present time travelling back and forth, endeavouring to see if it is possible to effect some sort of agreement. I do not want to be discouraging, but I do not take too much stock in the eleventh hour activities of this government in connection with trade agreements, any more than the working people of this country are taking too much stock in the unemployment insurance measure which was brought down during

this session and which has proved to be such a hollow echo of the announcements made on the public platform. The people of this dominion have pretty well in mind the attitude of this government with regard to the exchange and tariff restrictions that have been imposed in the last three or four years. Business men will not soon forget the plight in which they found themselves and the desperate situation which resulted in employees being thrown on the streets because the business men could not because of the uncertainties of the tariff policy of this government make plans in order to carry on their enterprises. That point is made very effectively, not by anyone in politics but by a man who is known pretty well all over this dominion and respected by the business community. It appears in the annual address made by President McLeod of the Bank of Nova Scotia, which can be found in the Financial Post of January 26, 1935. He said:
I will not attempt to describe here the mesh of tariffs, quota regulations, manipulations of currencies, exchange controls and exchange clearing arrangements by means of which all international trade, including our own, is being hampered to-day. No language at my command could exaggerate the destructive influence of these restrictions or the need for removing them as soon as possible. All countries including our own have played a part in weaving this mesh of repressive measures. All are more or less responsible for the present obstacles to trade. All must cooperate in the removal of them_ if the commerce of nations is again to start moving freely.
It is still true to say that we are only moving in world commerce two-thirds of the goods that were so moved five years ago.
If Mr. McLeod were referring to Canada he would say only one-half.
It logically follows from this that a large proportion of the workers employed in the world's export industries five years ago- workers who should now be making goods for exchange one with another-remain unemployed.
That is the situation in Canada. If my hon. friends on the other side had devoted themselves a little more assiduously to keeping the channels of trade open they would not have had the railway deficits and the special grants for unemployment relief that they have had.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to refer to a less sombre picture presented by my hon. friend in his budget speech; that is the reference which he makes to improved conditions in this country. That should have awakened the sleepers on his side of the house. The minister claimed that business was improving, and we

The Budget-Mr. Ralston
on this side say Amen, so mote it be. But obviously there ought to be some time when gains should be registered. We cannot go along all the time at the very bottom, and while it is a matter of satisfaction to know that our industrial .production is increasing in physical volume it seems to me we should make some comparison with countries other than ourselves. It is no use for us to go down into the sub-cellar and then, because we get to the first floor of our own house, say we are making progress. Let us compare ourselves with our neighbours all around us. In regard to the physical volume of production the best my hon. friend can say is we have actually reached the position we occupied last May; in other words, we are not losing much. Last May, he says, we were in the position we occupy to-day so far as physical volume is concerned; we went down, and now we are up again. All right; let us praise anyone who is entitled to praise for that, but it certainly does not indicate a very substantial advance. I submit that comparisons with other countries are perhaps more informative to Canadians who want to know the truth. My hon. friend makes comparisons with other countries; at page 2126 of unrevised Hansard he compares industrial production in Canada with that in other countries, but he makes a most peculiar comparison. He does not compare the volume of industrial production in Canada with other countries; he does not compare the amount of increase in industrial production in Canada with that in other countries. What he does is this: He says "I take January 1, 1933; I take an index figure as to the volume of industrial production in each of the countries referred to, and then I take, not the actual increase, but a percentage of the increase, and I say that Canada heads the list." Let us be glad that Canada does head the list in that respect, Mr. Speaker; but whether we can really rejoice depends on what position Canada occupied on January 1, 1933. Was she on a par with these other countries? If she was, and if her physical volume of production increased by a greater percentage than the others, then she is outstripping them.
I obtained the figures on industrial production as of January 1, 1933, the very figures used by my hon. friend, and here they are. Mr. Speaker, I call your attention to the fact that this shows that Canada was next to the bottom among the sixteen countries for which figures are given. If Canada was practically at the bottom is it any great wonder that Canada improved more than the others, if
she was going to keep her place in world trade at all? Yet the only comparison given by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance with regard to Canada's progress is a comparison with other countries taking Canada as at January 1, 1933, when she was next to the bottom in industrial production. Then he says she has improved more than the rest. Canadians are not those from whom unpleasant facts should be concealed. The people of this country were born optimists, but they were born realists as well. subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend will have an opportunity of making his speech and I think it will take all of his time to deal with the {joints I have raised in connection with the export trade of Canada. I have given, him sixteen countries to think about and he will see what the relative exports are for 1928 and 1935, 1932 and 1935 and the relative total trade for 1930 and 1935.
My hon. friend has made a point in connection with United Kingdom trade. I find -perhaps the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hanson) has these figures in his department-that our share of United Kingdom imports for the year ending September 30, 1932, just before the Ottawa agreements were made, was 5-20 while our share for the year ending September 30, 1934. was 6-33 In other words there was an improvement of one and one-half per cent. My hon. friends will say that this was due to the Ottawa agreements. It was not a very large increase and I think when a comparison is made between 1932 and 1934 it will be found that there are obvious causes other than the Ottawa agreements ' for the increase in imports into Great Britain from Canada. In the first place the buying power of Great Britain has been immeasurably improved by the rise of the pound; in the second place, the financial position of the British people was greatly improved in 1934 as compared with 1932.	If my
hon. friends are so proud of the Ottawa agreements, why has the motion of the hon. member for Toronto-Searborough (Mr. Harris) been allowed to die? That motion offered an opportunity for my hon. friends to have a vote on these agreements. Although I understood that we were to get that opportunity, it has not come. All that we get in the budget speech are a few general statements with regard to the increased trade with Great Britain. The difficulty is that my hon. friends know perfectly well that if the Dunning budget of 1930 had been in effect every item of trade which has moved
The Budget-Mr. Ralston

between Great Britain and this country would have moved under the generous provisions of that budget; it would not have required any bargaining at Ottawa to insure the flow of trade between these two great countries. From 1920 on we had a two to one preference as far as our trade with Great (Britain was concerned; we sold them $4,000,000,000 worth of goods and we bought only $2,000,000,000 worth from them. Our relations with Great Britain were extremely good. But then my hon. friends came along with their bargaining attitude. The Prime Minister when he was leader of the opposition used to stand in his place and declare that Great Britain would get nothing from us unless there was a quid for our quo; we would give nothing unless Great Britain gave us something in return. Where has that policy gone in the light of this budget? This seems to be another recantation. We find in this budget that forty-seven items in the British preference have been reduced without Great Britain being asked for anything in return. This budget indicates a complete repudiation of that policy which was advocated so strenuously by the present government from this side of the house. My friends have given these things and they do not indicate that Great Britain is to give anything for these concessions, comparatively small though they may be. This is another instance in which they have apparently seen the light.
Practically every year hon, friends opposite applaud the fact that the Minister of Finance is able to show a favourable balance of trade. This balance was $134,000,000 this year and $145,000,000 last year. I suppose I must repeat myself, but I contend as I have contended before that the benefits of a balance of trade depend altogether upon how that balance is brought about. If it is brought about by reason of larger exports it is a good thing, because then you have the substance wherewith to buy and trade. But if it is brought about by starving yourself for the things you need through a restriction of imports, then the balance of trade is nothing to boast of. This is the sort of balance which is represented by this budget. I notice the Minister of Trade and Commerce is taking notes and I assume he is to follow me in this debate. I should like to quote from a publication issued by his own bureau. In a statement covering the years 1926 to 1932 this publication states that "Balance of trade figures are frequently misinterpreted due to the persistence of the doctrine long ago exploded that a nation's trade is necessarily in a healthy state when exports exceed imports, necessitating the import of gold to make up the difference." I

should also like to quote from another publication which I believe some of my hon. friends will regard as an authority. I quote from the Financial Post of February 9, 1935, as follows:
Most of the debtor countries of the world have increased their so-called favourable balances of trade since the depression began. No doubt, in all of these countries, the politicians are pointing to this achievement as an evidence of the prosperity created by the particular .policies invoked by those politicians. A favourable balance of trade, if it were the result of a large volume of inward and outward transactions, might be something to crow over. But a very small total trade showing a favourable balance is no evidence in itself of prosperity in a country.
And further down:
But it is suggested that the current tendency to use a favourable balance of merchandise trade as an index of a country's prosperity is based on economic errors so gross as to be something of a political crime when politicians and after-dinner speakers utilize the device.
I submit that in view of the fact that the average total trade of this country for the last five year period has been only one-half of the average total trade for the previous five year period and because this favourable balance of trade has been produced by a restriction of imports rather than by an increase of exports, it is not necessarily evidence of a healthy state of trade in this country.
I pass over very briefly a matter to which I have referred at greater length on previous occasions. My hon. friend and his predecessor have repeatedly indulged in predictions as to what might be the result of the year's transactions. The hon. gentleman's predecessor, the Prime Minister, used to lecture those of us on this side of the house with regard to the responsibility of a Minister of Finance who ventured a forecast which proved to be in any substantial measure out when the results of the year's operations were known. He indicated that the Chancellor of the Exchequer was held to the strictest accounting in connection with any predictions he made. As I have had occasion to point out in this house before, my right hon. friend in 1931 predicted that the figures which he presented would indicate a balancing of the budget by a substantial margin. Well, he had a deficit of $81,000,000. In 1932 the present minister predicted that " reductions in expenditure and probable additions to revenue would represent a complete balancing of the budget on ordinary account " -these are his words-and he had a deficit of $53,000,000. I left him in the hands of his leader. Then in 1933 he predicted a surplus of $2,000,000 and he had a deficit on ordinary account alone of $24,100,000. This year he has

The Budget-Mr. Ralston
done a little better; gradually he has come up the scale. Last year he predicted a surplus of $8,800,000 to apply on extraordinary expenditures, and he reports a surplus of $2,700,000 on what he calls ordinary account. You can have surpluses if you leave out enough obligations, and to achieve his result my hon. friend has left out unemployment relief, railways, the construction program-in fact, he has left out about everything except what could be regarded as bare operating expenses. It is very different from the days when budgets were presented by the predecessor of the hon. gentleman and of the Prime Minister, when the accounts showed definite surpluses year after year, piling up to the amount of $257,000,000. All that my hon. friend says about his estimate is this. He says, "After we get through we have a deficit of $117,700,000." But he tells us to cheer up because the deficit for the previous year was $133,500,000, and that this year's figures indicate an over all improvement of $15,800,000. In other words, although we are not better we are less bad-$1:17,000,000 deficit this year but last year it was worse. I have had occasion before to deal with the question of the public debt, and on this occasion I feel-in fact, I know-that the situation is much more serious than it has ever been in the past. My hon. friend has a way of computing increases in the debt which may >be all right so far as bookkeeping is concerned but which, according to some whom he regards as very high authorities, is absolutely incorrect as representing the accurate debt condition of the country.
My hon. friend shows in his budget speech this year an increase in the net debt, since the end of 1929-30, of $669,900,000, and he says that, included in that, is $83,000,000 for the year 1930-31. And this, he says, should not be charged to the government. I say to him, what I said to his leader in 1931: You are responsible for the year 1930-31 except for the first four months, inasmuch as you had full opportunity to cancel any expenditures you wanted to cancel. All that had been done was that parliament had voted the money.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The question is whether
the deficit of $83,000,000 for the year 1930-31 should be charged to my hon. friend's administration. My hon. friend, as usual, has included it; he has not quibbled about it, because as I have pointed out, after the first four months my hon. friends had full charge, and the Minister of Railways confirms me now when he says that they cut out many items amounting to $75,000,000. We have therefore no quarrel on that score. They had control and they took control, and if there was a deficit at the end of the year they are responsible for it. The Liberal budget for 1930-31 had included $440,000,000. Now note. This budget, according to the Minister of Railways, was cut down by $75,000,000, and the next year the government, of which the Minister of Railways was a member, budgeted not for $440,000,000 less $75,000,000 but for $430,000,000, only $10,000,000 less than the Liberals had done the year before. So that it would rather indicate that they were fairly well satisfied with the 1930-31 budget that had been brought down by the Liberals.
The question I put to you, Mr. Speaker, is this: Is $669,900,000 the correct figure foi the increase in the debt including the 1930-31 year as being under the Conservative administration? I say that, on the authority of the Prime Minister and on the authority of the hon. gentleman who occupies the position of Minister of Justice at the present time, that is not the correct figure. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice, in a speech in 1929, when he was occupying the position I now occupy, made this statement in reply to the budget:
We have never had very serious controversy about the funded debt of the country, but I am glad to note that in his speech last Friday the minister for the first time took serious account of what we know as the funded or bonded debt or, as he put it in his remarks, the dead weight debt of the Dominion of Canada. That, after
The Budget-Mr. Ralston

all, is the important item in the financing of this country. The neit debt is not a matter of the greatest consequence; in England they never refer to it all. There they use the one term "dead weight debt," and I am glad that the minister has used that term on this occasion, because that is the debt which counts. lit is the amount for which the government of this country has issued in solemn form its bonds and obligations, signed, sealed and delivered, which bonds are now held by people who have invested in our securities. These bonds have to be paid at maturity, and in the meantime interest must be met. They therefore constitute the real burden which the people of this country are compelled to carry.
The net debt is comparatively unimportant; it is a matter very largely of bookkeeping and depends upon how you see fit to estimate the value of your assets. We have assets that are certainly good liquid assets, but we have a lot of assets in this country which we carry as non-active assets, and if you want to transfer some of these mouractive assets to the active list you can immediately decrease your net debt. It is. I say, a matter largely of bookkeeping. But the debt which counts is the dead weight debt.
Note that, Mr. Speaker, it is the "dead weight " debt which he says counts. Then the Prime Minister speaking from about the same position in 1928 said this, as reported in Hansard of that year on page 1246;
May I venture to point out, sir, that it should not be difficult to ascertain what the debt of the country is, and I Say further that there is no need to talk about "net" debt or "gross" debt. The proper term to apply is funded debt, and the funded debt of Canada means "tlhe mortgage on the farm." Now if She mortgage on the farm is $5,000, payable the 1st of January, 1929. and you have in your current account at the bank $1,000 which must be used to pay taxes, for seed grain and various other demands, at the end of the year the $1,000 may be partly or wholly exhausted, but the mortgage on the farm still remains $5,000 and must be treated as such.
There are two hon. gentlemen who do not talk about net debt, and yet that is what the present Minister of Finance talks about all the time. He says that there is an increase in the net debt of $669,000,000 from 1930 to 1935. I quote these authorities as indicating that that is not the correct practice according to his own colleagues. These are some of the things which are included in assets as shown on the balance sheet on page 1984 of Hansard and which would enter into the calculation of the net debt;
Loans to provinces	 $74,649,000
That is counted as a cash item. The question is whether those loans can be realized or not.
Loan to Roumania	 $23,969,000
That is counted as a cash asset.

I want to be quite fair; on the other hand there are superannuation funds and cash, but the point is that there is a definite balance on the assets side due to the building up of items such as those I mentioned a moment ago.	*
If we take then the funded debt, the "mortgage on the farm," what is the increase in debt under this government? During the five years of Liberal rule from 1925 to 1930 there was a total reduction of $257,000,000; I will not give the odd thousands. The funded debt on March 31, was as follows:

The difference between $812,000,000, which is the increase in the funded debt, in the mortgage on the farm, and the $669,000,000 to which my hon. friend refers, is a mere matter of $143,000,000, and what is that between friends? The interest on the increased debt of $812,000,000 is, as the house will realize, something like $32,000,000 to $33,000,000, or $2.50 to $3 a head for every man, woman and child in the dominion. It means that the increase in the funded debt for this year, 1934-35, is the largest that has ever been under my right hon. friend's administration, or $218,000,000. Do you wonder that I say that the situation with regard to the debt is serious when we find an increase of $812,000,000 in five years in the funded "dead weight" debt of the dominion?
My hon. friends opposite have said something about conversion. The Minister of Finance in his budget speech spoke about conversion loans, saying that there has been a reduction in interest charges. That is so, but as is pointed out by the dominion statistician, Doctor Coats, in a letter to one of the members of parliament:

The Budget-Mr. Ralston
Refundings which have taken place in the past four years have reduced the interest charges upon previously existing national debt by something Like $14.600,001) although this has been largely offset by increases in principal of our national obligations.
We are all glad that the rate of interest has been reduced, but a conversion loan does not mean anything so far as relieving us of interest charges is concerned, if the next minute we start in to borrow more money. The conversion loan of which my hon. friend rather boasts in his budget speech is nothing new; all it means is that the government, just like an individual, finds the goods it has to sell have a favourable market and it goes out and .sells them at a higher price. There is no (magic about that; there is nothing but good business judgment. I remember that conversion loans were effected under the former administration by which some $5,000,000 of interest was saved. This is therefore not an extraordinary transaction. We congratulate the government on having made the conversion; it was the proper thing to do in order to reduce the interest rate, but there is nothing specially outstanding about it in the way of business acumen or financial skill. So, while the rate has been reduced, while we have been able to sell government bonds at a higher price, we have had to make more loans and [DOT]the result is that the reduction in our interest charges is largely nullified. But the point that troubles me and I believe troubles the .people generally is that the reason the government is able to get cheap money is that there is a lack of confidence by investors in industry and commercial enterprises. A government bond is the best thing the people can get and therefore they put their money into it. The banks are holding over fifty per cent of their liquid assets in government bonds at the present 'time and this money is not going into industry. Cheap money for the government means that confidence has been lost or has not been restored in connection with industrial and commercial enterprises. That is the point which should trouble Canadians although rejoicing in the fact that the interest rate is being reduced so far as our national debt is concerned. I would rather see relief from the interest loan brought about in the way it was in the five years before 1930 when it was accomplished by paying off principal, not leaving any hangover whatever, when $257,000,000 of public debt was paid off entirely and the interest load reduced accordingly.
In that same connection I want to discuss a matter which it seems to me ought to occupy almost paramountly the attention of the public authorities of this country, and that is this whole matter of public finance. My hon. friend has mentioned, for the purpose of drawing the attention of the country to it, a possible scheme for refunding or dealing in a broad and comprehensive way with the whole matter of the public finance of the dominion, and has raised the question whether or not that can be done by what he speaks of as a loan council, or whether it could be done better through the more elastic organization, and the assistance I presume he means, of the central bank. I say to him that I agree that there should be something done by way of collaboration, by way of consultation, with regard to public financing in Canada. I am doubtful, and I think he is, whether the provinces would agree to federal control of
The Budget-Mr. Ralston

finance. I think he makes that fairly clear in his speech. But I feel that there is a possibility of having some sort of organization whereby there will be, nob control, but whereby in the first instance there will be consultation and study and working together rather than a degree of rigidity or authority. The point is that the dominion authorities apparently have admitted that the finances of the provinces are of vital interest to the dominion. I am one who has not been so sure that that is correct. Sometimes I have felt that the Prime Minister-I speak of him particularly because he is taking special interest in these things-has gone perhaps further than was necessary in that regard. I feel satisfied as one citizen of the dominion that he went altogether too far in protecting the credit of the dominion when he gave guarantees for Newfoundland. Whether or not that applies to the guarantees for the provinces of Canada I am not prepared to say. But we have in these accounts this fact, that the dominion of Canada, for better or for worse, has admitted some interest in the credit of the provinces, in view of the fact that there have been guarantees given in respect of provincial obligations to the extent of $74,000,000. If that is the case I submit that the time has come for some concerted and definite and serious attempt to put the public finances of the dominion on a sounder basis. It may be that my hon. friend is correct, and that the Bank of Canada may afford a nucleus for that organization. I believe that the provinces will have to be willing and enthusiastic participants before the thing can be a success. Interest charges on municipal, provincial and federal obligations are all paid by the same people and out of the same pocket, there is no such thing as separating the citizen of the Dominion of 'Canada from the citizen of any province or of any municipality. They are all one and all pay these taxes. Obviously since there is a disparity between the interest load of the different provinces it may be possible that there is a difference in the borrowing power and in the advisability of borrowing on the part of the different provinces. In some provinces there may be a possibility of public works that are nearer self-liquidating and of more productive capacity than in others. But if the credit of the various component parts of the dominion is affected by the action of others then the financial operations of each are of concern to the others. And if the dominion is concerned with possible unsound finance of the provinces I think the provinces have a right to say as well that they are concerned with possible unsound finance of the dominion, and that they
I-Mr. Ralston.]
should meet in the first instance as willing and enthusiastic participants rather than simply to meet under federal authority.
I therefore submit that it would be good common sense, good business, good government, for all concerned to apply their minds to the formation of some organization, for which I have suggested for want of a better name, ithat of public finance council. In that connection I am not suggesting the setting up of any super board, I am speaking of an organization formed of representatives of those concerned. This council ought to have, first, the power and opportunity of considering the great problem of refunding and lightening the burden of interest on loans already effected; second, of considering the wisdom of further borrowings and the capacity of the citizens to carry the burden; third, the effect of further borrowings on the credit of the constituent members represented on this council; fourth, and this is most important, the orderly offering and marketing of public issues. We have seen too often the provinces, the municipalities and the dominion rushing to get to the money market first in order to catch the opportunity of getting rid of their issues, leaving the others to drag. Again it seems to me that such a council could well consider standards of administration and efficiency respecting not only capital but current expenditures. And I want to make this point; I have never been a believer in centralization, I believe rather in decentralization and in preserving the pride and esprit de corps of the provinces and the municipalities. But I believe in working together in sound consideration of common problems because the political divisions of this country cannot live to themselves alone any more than nations can. We have tried that experiment in recent years and found it a dismal failure. Therefore in connection with this particular passage in the budget speech I believe that the getting together of a representative body in Canada constituted to suit our particular conditions, would work not only without injury to the local esprit de corps but with distinct benefit to the pride, self-respect and self-confidence of the citizens of every part of the dominion.
Now I come to a more contentious subject, as indicated by the fact that my hon. friend the Minister of Railways rose a few moments ago. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance on this occasion, as he has previously and as have his predecessors, rather treats the Canadian National Railways as a drag on the wheels, as something which comes in at the last minute to take all the joy out of life, to

The Budget-Mr. Ralston
take all the cream off the milk. In computing his deficit this year he first shows his surplus of I think $2,700,000, then proceeds to take off something for unemployment relief, something for capital expenditure, and1 for everything else, and finally brings in $48,000,000 for the Canadian National Railways as the last straw.
I submit that we cannot too often put before this house and the people of the country the position of the Canadian National Railways and of our railway problem. I am not going into it at length today, I- have discussed it before in this house, but I want to remind the house that the situation is this: There have been large commitments and advances by Canada on account of the roads which now comprise the Canadian National Railways; the Canadian National railway system is a combination, a conglomeration of what were regarded as almost junk railways, that it is as if you had taken three or four carts and taken a wheel off one,, a pair of shafts from another, a box off another and put them all together and made one cart and then proposed that that cart should do the work and pay the carrying charges of the four carts which originally composed it. It cannot be done. It is no use to set the Canadian National Railways up in a corner and say that that railway as a system is what is losing our money. It is not fair to the railway or to the finances of the country or to ourselves who have put the Canadian National Railways in that position. I say, as I said to the Minister of Railways, speaking of capital expenditure from 1921 to 1930, everyone in the house voted for it; everyone patted Sir Henry Thornton on the back; everyone-cities, municipalities, provinces, corporations, individuals and the dominion-was spending money, and the man who could spend the most money was the most popular man, the man who was doing the biggest things for his country. There is no use coming along now and talking about what has gone by; we all voted for it. Now the question is what we are going to do about it when the time comes to pay the bill.
My hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) speaking from his place in this house in. 1928, at a time when the Canadian National Railways had a deficit of $5,516,000 after paying interest to the public, said at page 1122 of Hansard:
Nobody will pretend-not the Minister of Railways, for he knows too well, nor the Minister of Finance-that this government or any member of it is entitled to a particle of credit for the improved showing made in connection with the Canadian National Railways. The management of the road is supposed' to be entirely divorced from government control. It is under the absolute control, so far as management goes, of Sir Henry Thornton and his board,
without government interference, and they are entitled to the full credit for the result obtained -$125,090,060 of relief for the treasury of Canada in four years.... The real fact is that the finance minister and the Minister of Railways are endeavouring to appropriate to themselves the credit that is due to Sir Henry Thornton. They are endeavouring to bask in the reflected glory of the president of the Canadian National Railways without there being the slightest foundation for their claiming any credit for his achievement ... the point which I desire to make is this, that if credit be due to anyone in respect to the reduction of the net debt of the dominion, that credit is directly due to the management of the Canadian National Railways; for the improved showing which they have been able to make and for the relief which for the last four years they have been able to afford to the treasury of Canada. Without one move of the hand or one stroke of the pen by the finance minister or any of his colleagues, Sir Henry Thornton and his board have accomplished that feat, and to them credit is due, and to them the thanks of the country should be returned.
That was in 1928. Now I quote from Hansard for 1929, at page 742. In that year the result of the operations of the Canadian National Railways was a deficit of $3,185,000 after paying interest due the public. The present Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) said:
The result of operations for last year was very gratifying, and T would ask the Minister of Finance to note that the treasury of this country has been relieved very substantially for the last four or five years through the successful operation of Canada's national railway system. On January 1, 1924, an announcement was made by the president that for the first time in its history the national system had produced a net revenue over operating expenses, for the year 1923, amounting to $4,155,000; in 1924 that revenue had increased to $18,000,000; in 1925, it had increased again to $33,000,000; in 1926 the revenue was $48,000,000; in 1927 it dropped' back to $42,000,000; and for 1928 we have the wonderful result of a surplus in net operating expenses amounting to $58,000,000. It will take $50,000,000 of that amount to pay the interest on the bonds which the public hold. I understand the management of the road will pay that interest this year, and will still have on hand a balance of $8,000,000 for other purposes.
That was the attitude in which the present Minister of Justice, representing the Conservative party, viewed the Canadian National Railways at that time. Before I am through I will give the house the benefit of another extract. They regarded it as the child of the management; they were congratulating the management on the way it was getting on. There was no talk then of spending too much.
These are the points, Mr. Speaker. First, these roads are a conglomeration of a number of bankrupt roads. Second, they are a combination of the policies of all parties,
The Budget-Mr. Ralston

not of one party alone. The Minister of Railways has come to that conclusion himself ; he expressed that view in a speech he made in Ingersoll last fall. According to the report in the Toronto Globe of April 10, the minister said:
Turning to the railway situation in Canada, the minister reviewed the construction of the transcontinental line, declaring that each party should go fifty-fifty in the matter of blame for this.
All three transcontinental roads were the policies of everybody. I made that statement in the house on one occasion and someone interrupted to say that it was not so. After that I had occasion to look up the records, and I think I convinced even the doubters that that was the case, and that the three transcontinental railways were advocated and supported by no less a gentleman than the Prime Minister. Sir Robert Borden approved the building of a second road, another transcontinental railway, in the amendment which he moved to the Grand Trunk Pacific Act, in 1904. The Grand Trunk Pacific and the National Transcontinental were built soon after. In 1912-13 a Conservative government granted a subsidy in order to permit the completion of the Canadian Northern through to the coast. That made the third transcontinental railway. This is what my right hon. friend the present Prime Minister said during the course of that debate, according to Hansard for June 3, 1913, at page 11777:
Mr. Bennett: Do not we require a third transcontinental line as a spout for western grain? And hence is not the construction of the road from Fort William to the seaboard absolutely essential if the value of the other lines is to be maintained?
Then further down he said:
I suppose the hon. gentleman will admit that the railways had to run parallel; they went through the same pass; it was a physical necessity.
That is the road in connection with which my right hon. friend indicated that he almost felt ashamed, as he went past Sir Wilfrid Laurier's monument, to think how far Sir Wilfrid had gone astray in connection with the railway policy of this country. All three railway lines were advocated and supported by all parties in this country.
In the next place, Mr. Speaker, the advances by the government have been wiped out by common consent. Ini a passage which I will read in a moment or two, quoting from the remarks of the present Minister of Justice, my hon. friend regarded the money which was paid by this country for the roads making up the Canadian National Railways as a bookkeeping rMr. Ralston.!
item, and he thought no endeavour should be made to have it paid back. The sum of about $1,700,000,000 incurred when these roads were taken over before the Liberals came into power in 1922 is the big item in connection with our railway obligation. Fourth, the capital expenditures were approved by all parties in the house. Fifth, the revenue losses -and I want this to be noted-on the Canadian National are no greater than the revenue losses on the other great railway system in this country; they run along neck and neck. The railway is well operated. Sixth, the capital is represented by bonds which are an annual charge, and that is the difference between the financing of the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific. The Canadian National has every dollar of its capital shown in the way of bonds, with fixed charges. The Canadian Pacific has, besides debentures, stock, on which it is not required to pay dividends unless there is a profit. Seventh, the management was approved by all parties.
The railway is the property of the people of Canada, taken over under the authority of their representatives. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance, as I say, treats it as a sort of drag on the wheel, and the Prime Minister made a most astounding statement a short time ago. Speaking in Toronto, as reported in the Ottawa Journal of January 29, 1935, the Prime Minister said;
It far transcends the importance of any political party-it is your problem-not Bennett's and not the government's.
I thought my right hon. friend was running the government, and I thought this was one of the problems with which the government had to deal. According to the budget speech there is an item for that purpose, and I say to my right hon. friend that he cannot get rid of his obligations as head of the Government in that way. He cannot throw up his hands and say, " I have no responsibility for the Canadian National Railways," nor can this government say so. They should tackle the railway problem courageously,, and not pass the buck as they do. I say the Canadian National Railways are part of Canada's national equipment. They were undertaken, put together and financed by the people of this country, and the government of Canada have no right to throw the problem out of the windbw, or to attempt to get rid of it by leaving it on the door step of the nation. I say also-and in this I may be treading on delicate ground, but I am going to say it-that the chairman of the Canadian National Railways has just as much right to stand up and tell the people of the Dominion of Canada about the Canadian

The Budget-Mr. Ralston
National Railways as the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway has to tell them about his road. I say that has not been recognized by this government. Some statements were made in Halifax, but apparently the chairman of the board of trustees of the Canadian National Railways was promptly told-

I ask my hon. friend to provide the machinery for an arbitral tribunal and see whether they will or not. As a matter of fact the chief commissioner is supposed to preside over an arbitral tribunal, but at the present time there is no chief commissioner and the position has been left vacant a long time. If my hon. friend would inquire-and I am not so sure he has not now the information-I think he would find that some applications are pretty nearly ready, or probably
have been ready for some time and something could be done, if there were some machinery whereby they could be presented.
My hon. friend has asked me what to do. I say to him that he should try the legislation he brought down two years ago. Then we will see if this thing works out, if it is possible for men to get around a table, and to find out whether or not there may be certain portions of the roads, in one place or another, where the services might be undertaken by one and abandoned by the other. That has not been tried, at all. There has not been one blessed thing done, so far as I can find out, with regard to lessening of expenditures as contemplated by that legislation. But my hon. friend comes here year after year complaining about the deficit of the Canadian National Railways. The Prime Minister goes to Toronto, throws up his hands and says, "It is your problem." I submit the Canadian National Railways have not been treated fairly. Why do they not try out the legislation which they themselves provided and which, I believe, they thought would work at the time.
Let me say a further word more about the railways, I have suggested one solution. My second solution is this-perhaps my second should have been the first; probably the order should have been changed. However the solution is, that if the trade of this country could be improved, and if my hon. friends opposite would adopt a policy which would move the wheat, if they would develop external trade and thus provide freight for our railways from coast to coast they would probably get somewhere near to solving the problem, just as the Minister of Justice throught our railway problem was being solved in 1928-29 when we nearly balanced the payment of interest to the public.
On this point regarding trade policy as affecting railways let me now quote the president of the Bank of Nova Scotia, who indicates just what he believes is the real trouble behind our railways in Canada. Here is what he states:
I shall have something to say presently regarding the strangulation of the world's trade, which we have -witnessed during the past few years, and its consequences, direct and indirect. It suffices here to remark that there have been no more unfortunate victims than the Canadian railways, of the passion for economic nationalism, which has been dominating and still in a measure, dominates the world.
That is the trouble with the railways in Canada to-day " unfortunate victims of the passion for economic nationalism". Take the nachinery which has been provided, and if that machinery does not provide a solution
The Budget-Mr. Ralston

probably my second suggestion would. But in addition to what I have said may I remind my hon. friend, when he asks what I have to suggest, that the leader of my hon. friend while sitting in opposition used to say, "as Mr. Gladstone once said, When I am called in I will prescribe."

speechtext: It won't be long now.

speechtext:
I said I would quote one other reference made by the Minister of Justice and I find it at page 743 of Hansard for 1929. This is what my hon. friend thought of the Canadian National Railways at that time-and I suppose he expressed the opinion of the Minister of Railways and Canals:
But what about the money it owes to the dominion treasury? The minister intimates that the sum of $32,000,000 odd is owed this year to the government for interest. It is put down in the books as a debt of the railway, but is purely a book-keeping transaction, and I presume it will be added to the $1,258,000,000 which the company owed to us at the beginning of the year, making the total indebtedness of the system to the dominion treasury about $1,300,000,000 and to the public about $1,000,000,000.
In this respect, however, to the National railways we on this side of the house are all optimists. We look upon that railway as practically our own infant and our own creature.
He continues at page 745:
Now, when this wonderful Canadian National railway system has more than justified itself, now, that it is rapidly becoming in the nature of a great national asset, now that we may look forward to a day, not perhaps in my lifetime, buit in the lifetime of some here, when this system will start repaying the government of Canada part at least of the money it owes to the treasury, to the day when it will have a clean sheet, as it ultimately will have, in regard to its bonded indebtedness to the public; now that the system is in this, a thoroughly prosperous condition-
Under a Liberal government.
-this government desires to treat it as its own creature. Whereas in 1919 it tried to cast it out as base-born, now it wants to consider it as its legitimate offspring, and to profit by its success. Let me say, in concluding my remarks on this phase of the subject, that the national railway system in this country constitutes a lasting monument to the ability and statesmanship and determination of a single man, a member of a former Conservative government, and subsequently Prime Minister of that government. It is to his ability and foresight, to his statesmanship and determination that the people of Canada are indebted for this wonderful system of national railways.
I suggest to my hon. friend that he might go to the present leader of the Senate and find out from him what to do about these railways, as according to the present Minister of Justice the national railways are a monu-

ment to his statesmanship and determination. Go to him and find out what his advice would be about the railways for which according to the Minister of Justice we are indebted to the present leader of the Senate.
Now we come to the budgeting for the next year-and here is where I have to find serious fault with my hon. friend. As best he could he has given us a report of what took place last year, and to some extent at least he has given a forecast of expenditures and receipts for the next year. Here again I would remind him, to use that well known phrase, that the Chancellor of the Exchequer in delivering his address to the British parliament is always held to "strictest account" for the extent to which he has been able to realize his expectations. At page 2168 of Hansard for 1931 this question was asked by the Prime Minister:
Will any hon. member on the other side of the house say that last year there was any estimate given of expected revenues? Was there any estimate given of expected expenditures? Was there any word given of a $75,000,000 deficit? What did they do? What the then government did was merely to bring down estimates for moneys to be raised by taxation without any estimate of what was -to be realized. I said frequently in this house in those days, and I now repeat, that not in any municipal council in this country would the people tolerate their mayor amid councillors conducting business without giving an estimate of expected expenditures and revenues for the current year. It is the basis of responsible government, it is the basis upon wibioh representative institutions have been established, and that responsibility can only attach when there is some estimate as to What is being received by the country from the taxation imposed...
My hon. friend has budgeted for a surplus of $21,500,000. But he says there will be some special expenditures the amounts of which he does not give. I should like to attempt to complete the budget; he has left some things out. There will be $6,000,000 on capital account, and how much for unemployment relief? Surely under this government there will be no necessity for unemployment relief. I shall not read that classic passage from the speech the Prime Minister delivered at Moncton during the 1930 campaign, but I will make mention of one made five years ago at Victoria. On June 17, 1930, he is reported to have said:
You have my promise that if the Conservative party is returned to power that as soon after July 28 as possible parliament will be called together to deal with the problem of unemployment by providing, not doles, but work and that legislative action will be taken to bring about the future security of our country and the well being of its people .... We cannot tolerate the dole. Men and women of this country want work, not charity.

The Budget-Mr. Ralston
Here is another speech which has not been quoted so often. At Quebec on July 14, he said:
There was no necessity for a conference on unemployment. The solution was too apparent. "What you want is work," he exclaimed, "not conferences, and you are going to get work." Unless bis promises to the people of Canada were kept if elected to office, Mr. Bennett said he wanted Quebec and other members of his parity to vote him out of office.
Of course that Moncton speech we all know so well is written in the copy books of the school children from Halifax to Vancouver. There were to be no doles but work. But now, after five years my hon. friend brings down a budget in which he proposes to spend a huge amount for unemployment relief. Compare the Prime Minister's remarks at Vancouver, Quebec and Moncton during the campaign in 1930 with what the Minister of Finance states in 1935:
Tile total number of individuals on relief, including dependents, was 1.229.935 in February Which is a decrease of 117,285 from February of last year, and of 265,031 from March, 1933.
Notwithstanding all the assistance given by government work, government projects, and relief construction, notwithstanding the enormous expenditures already made, these are the people on relief in Canada-or, at least, this number were on relief at the time this paragraph in the budget speech was prepared. As yet there has been no considered program with regard to unemployment and there has been no considered program with regard to relief. It has been helter skelter, hit or miss. One year it has been public works, another year it has been relief, another year it has been public works and relief; one year it has been a certain percentage of contribution by the provinces and municipalities, and then this has been changed; there has been no uniformity.
There never was a finer program given to the government than was included in the speech by Miss Charlotte Whitton to the Canadian Chamber of Commerce in Winnipeg. She pointed out the absolute necessity of a national relief council if there was to be any proper administration of relief in this country.
