speechtext:
My right hon. leader
points out that that policy was suggested by him at the first session in 1930, and he has repeated it year after year but to deaf ears. This matter must be treated from the dominion point of view. There should be some general, coordinated policy. It must be seen
to that standards are the same and that services furnished are similar. Consideration should be given to the needs of the individual but there should be no exodus from one part of the country to another in order to secure a higher scale of relief or more extensive relief benefits thus enabling the locality which is paying less to get rid of its obligation. These are things which have not been considered by this government, yet in 1935, when we have 1,229,000 on relief, my hon. friend comes down with his budget and says: "I cannot tell you how much we are going to pay for relief; I can just tell you that we are going to have a surplus of
S21,000,000 and we will have to pay relief out of that." We paid $49,000,000 for relief last year and my hon. friend says that there was a carryover from 1933 amounting to $9,000,000. Five million dollars was paid to Saskatchewan on account of drought relief and my hon. friend thinks that that may be paid back. However, I am striking that off with the $9,000,000. That makes $14,000,000 which leaves $35,000,000 which ought to be added to the estimated expenditures for the coming year.
What about the Public Works Construction Act? The total vote for this was approximately $40,000,000 but only $8,000,000 was spent last year. If this program is to be carried out it will be necessary to spend $32,000,000 this year, but that is not referred to in the budget forecast. The money will have to be got somewhere if it is to be spent this year and if my hon. friends do what we expect they will do, namely, start to erect a lot of public buildings and projects on the eve of the election. That is another $31,000,000. But is that all? There are rumors about an additional public works program. I do not know whether this is right; my hon. friend does not tell us anything about it in his budget speech. I thought that if this were so it would need an amount similar to that which was voted in last year's estimates. Perhaps it will not be this much, but I have put it in at an additional $40,000,000. The railway deficit is still to be provided for. My hon. friend takes an optimistic view about this. Last year the railway showed an surplus of $6,000,000 before the public interest was paid and he expects that next year the deficit will be reduced by $4,400,000. That leaves about another $44,000,000 to be provided for.
Lastly, there is the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited. Two years ago I suggested in this connection that $20,000,000 should be provided but the Prime Minister later indicated that there might be a loss of $15,000,000. I have put in $20,000,000. So
The Budget-Mr. Ralston

tve have 86,000,000 for capital expenditure, $35,000,000 for relief, 832,000,000 for a construction program, $40,000,000 for a further construction program, $44,000,000 for the railway deficit and $20,000,000 for a possible deficit in connection with the wheat transactions. This gives a total of $177,000,000, but I will make it $160,000,000, against which there is a surplus of only $21,000,000. There would seem to foe the possibility of our debt being increased next year by $125,000,000. So far under Conservative administration our funded debt has been increased by $812,000,000 and with this addition for next year it will have been increased by nearly one billion dollars. I think my hon. friend is quite right when he says in his speech at page 1989 of Hansard:
Meantime recovery will be hastened if we face our obligations courageously. To attempt to run away from them by failing at least to strive to pay our way, would not only retard recovery but this course would in the long run entail much greater sacrifice.
We should pay our way but we have not paid our way in any single year since this government came into office. I venture to predict that if this government stays in power we will continue not to pay our way. If we are to pay our way we must start doing things in a businesslike way, and I believe the people of Canada will see to this at the first opportunity. In the final result, the financial statement offered by my hon. friend is not a budget because he ignores entirely these items which are bound to come up for payment, with the possible exception of the added public works program.
I should like now to refer to the wheat-guarantee. I do not intend to take up much time in this connection as I understand we are to be given an opportunity to discuss this matter in the near future. On page 2149 of Hansard is a table of loans and guarantees made by the government. There is a loan to British Columbia, to Manitoba, to the Manitoba savings office, to the Algoma Steel Corporation, to the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation, to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and to the government of Newfoundland. Amounts appear opposite all these items, but the next item concerns the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited, and in this instance the amount is "unstated"- another blank cheque. I should like to refer for a moment to the transactions which gave rise to this guarantee. I shall do so very briefly, as in the very nature of things an opportunity should be given to discuss this matter before dissolution.
This guarantee was originally granted by order in council P.C. 2238 dated September 12,

1931. Hon. members will remember that in January, 1931, the Prime Minister issued a letter by which he guaranteed the advances made by seven banks to the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited in connection with the handling of the 1930 crop and the order in Council was passed nine months after. Mr. McFarland took over the job; in fact he took over two jobs. One was to dispose of the 1930 crop, and the other was to see that the market would not be unduly depressed by this action. I do not believe there has ever been a definite statement made by anyone in authority in connection with this matter, but the reports are that Mr. McFarland commenced his job by purchasing 75,000,000 bushels of wheat. When the Minister of Finance brought down his budget in 1932 mention was made of this guarantee, and more definite information was given at that time than has been given in any subsequent budget. On page 1759 of the Hansard of 1932, the Minister of Finance stated:
Based upon present market prices, the expectation is that, when -all accounts are settled, the Canadian. Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited, will be able to settle all advances without recourse being had to the dominions guarantee.
So in 1932 the minister was predicting that there would be no loss to the dominion on-account of the guarantees. During the fall session of 1932 this matter came up again and the Prime Minister is reported on page 1176 of Hansard as saying:
Except for the mention of the exact financial amount involved, which obviously it is difficult to give, I think I have answered all the questions asked.
Of course it was difficult to give the financial amount involved without giving the amount of wheat purchased. The dominion had guaranteed the loans made by the seven banks to the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited covering the full amount of the commitments made by Mr. McFarland in purchasing wheat. This matter was again before the house in 1933, and the Minister of Finance is reported on page 3455 of Hansard of that year as saying:
The question of ultimate liability will depend entirely upon the future course of wheat prices.
In March, 1934, the Prime Minister became a little more communicative; he indicated to the house that there might be a loss of $15,000,000. Now in 1935, just before the government goes to the country, the Minister of Finance gives us the laconic information that the amount of the guarantee is "unstated." And I now give the whole reference which appears in the present budget to this rather

important and somewhat large commitment of the Dominion of Canada to the banks of this country through Mr. McFarland. At page 1983 the minister says:
The guarantee of bank advances arising out of the operations of the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited in connection with the marketing of wheat, was continued.
Apart from the wheat guarantee, which is for an unstated amount and is subject to fluctuation from day to day, the aggregate of guarantees under the relief acts is $65,717 000 a decrease of $27,500,000 in the fiscal year. The amounts of the different guarantees are as follows:
And then he quotes the guarantees under the relief act and gives the list which I read a few minutes ago, concluding with " Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited," and under the column headed "Estimated principal amount of guarantee outstanding March 31, 1935 " appears the one word " unstated." I wish to make it clear-and I do not think there is need to emphasize it-that I am finding no fault with the government's action in connection with the first transaction of participating with the western wheat producer in an endeavour to dispose of the crop. That is not what we are objecting to. What I am objecting to is the method that has been adopted by Mr. McFarland as the dictator of Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited, and the method adopted by the Minister of Finance in this house with respect to the submission of this information, keeping the house entirely in ignorance of the liability involved and not even giving an estimate. I have no criticism of the objective which was aimed at originally, but what I have the strongest criticism to offer in respect of is the method and the motives which seem to have actuated Mr. McFarland in carrying out his mandate. This is a blanket guarantee, a guarantee which has been running for four years in favour of seven of the chartered banks of the dominion; and instead of the grain being disposed of which was supposed to be disposed of soon after the 1930 crop year, instead of seventy-five million bushels or so being disposed of, if the reports are correct, there is between two hundred and twenty-five and two hundred and forty million bushels of wheat on hand at the present time. That is the note which the dominion endorses. My objections are these. In 1933 when wheat went to a price substantially above what it had been, Mr. McFarland, instead of selling wheat held it-or if he did sell it he went into the market and bought again. That was a transaction which, I submit, had the effect of rank speculation on the part of the dominion, speculation with the money of the people of the country; and as my right hon.
The Budget-Mr. Ralston
leader suggests, it was done under an order in council which depended for its validity on the peace, order and good government provisions of the British North America Act-a rather remarkable situation, a situation which is not usual in any country I know of, that a peace, order and good government statute should be used for the purpose of speculation, taking the credit of the people of this dominion and putting it behind one man in order that he might deal with that credit, not for the benefit of the western wheat producer -and I shall show that in a moment-but for the possible eventual glorification of Mr McFarland and this government.
In the fall of 1933 wheat was pegged on the Winnipeg market, and pegged at the instance of Mr. McFarland, who was acting under the authority of this government. There is no doubt about it that he was the agent of this government; that has been abundantly shown in this house and in the committee on banking and commerce as well. My hon. friend the former Minister of Trade and Commerce, speaking in this house in 1933, made the following statement, as reported at page 3718 of Hansard:
The government authorized Mr. John I. Mo Fariamd, the head of the pool sales agency, to purchase grain for future delivery when it was necessary to do so in order to hold the market steady.
The evidence of Mr. Logan, the general manager of the Canadian Bank of Commerce, before the banking and commerce committee in March, 1934, as reported at page 133, was:
Since the 31st of July, 1931. the banks have loaned Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited such amounts as have been required to carry such quantities of wheat and/or contracts for future deliveries of wheat as in the estimation of the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited and with the approval of the Prime Minister have been necessary to ensure the orderly marketing of the Canadian wheat crop.
That would indicate, I should think, that Mr. McFarland was acting at the instance of this government; the government was the guarantor and he was acting under its authority. Mr. Logan says that it was with the approval of the Prime Minister that the banks made the advances. As I said wheat was pegged on the Winnipeg exchange in 1933 at the instance of Mr. McFarland who was to all intents and purposes the agent of the government. Now let me read what one gentleman thought of pegging a little earlier than 1933. Here is what the Prime Minister said in this house in 1931, as reported at page 781 of Hansard, referring to the government:

The Budget-Mr. Ralston

It did not peg the price; no government of which I am the head ever will. I have seen artificial prices placed upon commodities and whether that commodity be wheat or anything else, it matters not, I know the inevitable result. It cannot advantageously be done; it will not succeed. It may cau9e a temporary advantage, but that disappears. Look at the situation in the United States to-day. Mr. Legge, with all his vast experience, with all the millions and hundreds of millions of dollars that he has behind him, declared that the principle of artificial price fixing was unsound, and it has been abandoned.
Nevertheless wheat was pegged on the Manitoba exchange in 1933 at the instance of Mr. McFarland, he being to all intents and purposes the agent of the dominion government-a government that was going to see to it that wheat would never be pegged.
And then Mr. McFarland told us in March, 1934, before the banking and commerce committee, as reported at page 129 of the proceedings, that the position with regard to wheat was such that if there were a ten per cent increase in the price of wheat the government would be even with the market, or, to use his exact words, it would "create a condition where there would be no calls under government guarantees." In the banking and commerce committee we were trying to get a statement from Mr. McFarland, the representative of the government, as to what obligation was involved in order that we might know something about the country's financial commitments, and that was the nearest we could get, that ten per cent would relieve the government entirely. And the Prime Minister a few days after, at page 2057 of Hansard, said:
If the price of wheat were to rise ten per cent above what ft was to-day, the guariantor would be under no liability.
In other words, if wheat rose by ten per cent we could get out and the people of Canada's endorsement would be relieved. What happened after that announcement was made? May wheat was then over 67 cents, and on May 31, only two months after the Prime Minister had spoken, it was over 81 cents, and that was away above the ten per cent spread. And yet Mr. McFarland stopped selling wheat. What has been the result? The result has been that Argentine wheat has been going into Great Britain and that the Canadian producer is losing his market there. During the fall of 1934 shipments have been the smallest of any fall since 1929, and that notwithstanding the fact that Russia is out of t'he market and that the United States is taking a good deal of durum wheat, and frosted wheat for feed. I infer that the idea was that either Mr. McFarland or the government for whom he was acting wanted

to make a reputation as astute market operators and possibly to get some glory out of the distribution of the profits later. We find that in the fall of 1934 the prices of Canadian wheat in the British market were something like 22 cents above Argentina and something like 14 cents above Australia. What has been the result of the gambling attitude? In the first place the dominion as it wanted to do, shared with the western wheat producer in the responsibility for marketing the 1930 crop, and nobody finds any fault -with that action; both parties joined in approval of it. There has neveT been a word of criticism upon that score because everybody recognizes the importance of the western farmer as a producer, as a consumer and also as a citizen. What is the criticism? It is first from the point of view of the western farmer that the government instead of marketing the grain has virtually become his competitor. What do I mean by that? I mean that the government through Mr. John I. McFarland, who is its agent, becomes in effect the potential holder of 200,000,000 or
225,000,000 or 250,000,000 bushels of wheat that Should be off the market in order to enable the western producer to dispose of his 1935 crop. That quantity is still here; it is still in the hands of the Canadian government. The Canadian government cannot be depended upon to keep it forever. That wheat should have been cleared off the market just as the Argentine wheat was. In Argentina they kept the bins clear; they sold the Wheat, and the result is that in Argentina there is very little carry-over and their operation has come out practically square, due in some measure at least to the fact that there has been an advantageous exchange. Nevertheless the Argentine government saw to it that there would not be a great big pile-up and carry-over of wheat. That is not what has taken place in this dominion, and the result is that the government instead of helping the . Canadian farmer in effect stands in the market as his competitor.

Yes, and losing the market all the time. That brings me to the next point. We have been teaching the best customer of the Canadian producer to get along without our wheat; that is what has happened. The British miller, finding out more and more as he has that Canadian wheat is being held away above what he regards as the market price, is purchasing in other directions. I have before me a brief statement which I

propose to read, showing the shipments that have been made under a spread of twenty cents over the Argentine price and fourteen cents over the Australian price, indicating that the British miller, regardless of questions of patriotism, because he is as hardheaded as anybody else, is going to buy the cheapest wheat and is learning to get along without ours. I understand that from the time he made that statement, which was on February 16, something like 10,000,000 bushels of wheat a week would have to go out of this country to get -the carry-over down to Mr. McFarland's prediction before the new crop year. Therefore, for at least ten weeks prior to March 16 the shipments have averaged 1,900,000 bushels a week instead of an average of something like 10,000,000 bushels which should have been shipped if the bins are to be cleared to the extent Mr. McFarland predicted. First, the Canadian farmer finds this
92582-134J
wheat overhanging this market; second, he finds his customers buying somewhere else and third, he finds something else. If I may presume -for a moment to speak on behalf of the western farmer, what is going on out in the west is this: Mr. McFarland is absolute autocrat of the situation out there with the directors of the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited simply more or less figureheads. The cooperative spirit, the spirit in -which the western farmer takes some interest in -what are his own affairs, is being killed. The result is that Mr. McFarland is becoming the dictator of the wheat situation in the west with the western farmers' organization out of the picture. That is one of the most dangerous things which could happen in the Dominion of Canada, and particularly in Alberta and Saskatchewan. More dictatorship, as my hon. leader suggests! The ideas of the people who have had experience, who all their lives have been engaged in the grain business, who can contribute something and who have a real financial interest in the situation, are completely disregarded and a dictatorship is set up in the person of Mr. McFarland, who presumes to conduct the wheat business for the whole country 1
Let me quote an article from the Financial Post of August 19, 1933, with regard to this very situation. This is what the Post has to say about what was developing at that time. This was at the time when wheat had risen in the Canadian market and when Mr. McFarland did not sell, when wheat was held, as I submit, for speculative purposes. This is what the Post says:
But a new objective appeared to emerge when the price of wheat began to- rise some months ago, that of making a large profit. Parity newspapers began to talk of the government's huge profits in wheat. Government holdings, taken on under the excuse that there were no other purchasers in sight, were retained when other purchasers appeared and Clamoured to be allowed to buy. As a result, wheat prices soared to levels that could not be maintained, to levels that shut off our export business, and to levels from which there has been an inevitable reaction.
The profit th>a-t seemed to be almost in band has entirely or in large measure disappeared, but not before discussion began as to whose profit it was. It wras said to belong to the pools, presumably to the farmers who had wheat in the 1930 pool, the marketing of which was the nominal excuse for the continuance of the agency. Politicians began to calculate the possible effect on the next election of the distribution of some millions of dollars through the pool organization.
I have enumerated some of the effects on the western farmer. What about the effect on the country? It is simply this: the Min-
The Budget-Mr. Ralston

ister of Finance brings down his budget and our liabilities on account of the Canadian [DOT]Cooperative Wheat Producers are "unstated." The dominion is endorsing a note for an unlimited amount; its agent, the government, refuses to disclose the amount of the liabilities and how much wheat is on hand. This government proposes to go into the election, having committed the country to seven banks in respect of a transaction which is said to amount to between 200,000.000 and 240,000,000 bushels of wheat, and no one is to know what liability is involved! Without a statement from the Minister of Finance as to the extent of the present holdings and the prospective liability in respect of this wheat guarantee, this so-called budget is a delusion. I submit that any parliament which allowed this budget to pass without proper information would not be worthy of the name. Finally I submit that the unhappy position in which we find ourselves is due to lack of appreciation of the duty of the government to the wheat growers of western Canada and to the whole country to dispose of that wheat with all possible expedition and not to condone and support a huge gambling operation in the hope of being able to point to gains as evidence of efficient administration.
With regard to ways and means, my hon. friend makes some proposals in regard to taxation to which I want to refer briefly. He retains his virtual twenty-five per cent tax on sugar, a household necessity, but he reduces his tax on liquor by over forty per cent. I had hoped, and others on this side and I believe a good many on the other side had hoped, that the Minister of Finance had intended to cancel the sugar tax this year. We supposed he put it on as an emergency tax. He put on the gold tax, he said, in order to permit the sugar tax to be reduced by half; last year in making his statement to the house he said that to replace the revenue lost by the reduction of the tax on sugar it was proposed to levy a tax of ten per cent on gold. The gold tax is gone, but half of the sugar tax still remains. I think my hon. friend will find it very hard to explain to the people of Canada how he can collect a greater amount of taxes from liquor with lower rates of excise taxes and customs duties. It is peculiar that it is only being discovered just on the eve of an election that they can reduce the tax on liquor and at the same time maintain the revenue. Sugar, a necessity of life, bears a twenty-five per cent load, while the general sales tax is six per cent. My hon. friend has picked out this commodity for taxation without regard to the fact that it

bears on the masses of the people. Why? Simply because it is easy to collect. Seventeen millions were collected the first year, I think, and $8,000,000 or $9 000,000 last year- a very fine tax, but my hon. friend must remember, and the government must remember and the people of Canada will remember, who has to pay this enormous levy on a necessity of life.
With regard to the gold tax, my hon. friend remembers that last year we on this side of the house protested as vigorously as we could against the unfairness of the way in which this tax was to be levied, namely as a tax on production and not as a tax on profit. It was being levied on one of the basic products of this country, a commodity by the way which has probably done as much as any commodity to keep this country out of bankruptcy. My hon. friend and his leader after consideration accepted our suggestion, changed the gold tax and made it in effect a tax on profit by making it applicable only to mines which paid dividends. Now that gold tax comes off, and another tax takes its place, a tax half on the mine, and half on the shareholders. It remains to be seen what the effect of chat will be. I am a bit sceptical with regard to how this tax will emerge from the committee of ways and means. I have hardly ever known a tax proposed by this government that has emerged from that committee in the same form as it went in. My hon. friend always has to after his taxation proposals. I shall not be at all surprised if there is a change in connection with the gold tax-

speechtext:
I remember in 1931 an
income tax proposal was made the effect of which would have been that the tax on incomes in the higher brackets would be reduced, and that after a very vigorous attack by the former Secretary of State (Mr. Rin-fret), that resolution was withdrawn by the Prime Minister, because, as he indicated, of some personal affront which he had taken at the remarks which had been made. It has taken three years for the government to realize that what the former Secretary of State said was correct, and that here was a possible source of revenue in higher taxation of the higher incomes. Now, at the last session of this parliament, after a speech made by the

The Budget-Mr. Ralston
Prime Minister in Montreal recently, a tax is put upon two forms of income, first upon earned income amounting to over $14,000, and secondly on a form of income which is called investment income. I must say that this surtax on incomes is to say the least rather delicate on the higher incomes. It does not bear too heavily on them, having regard to the motives which were supposed to be behind it. Looking at the table of proposals I find that the man who has an income of between $14,000 and $20,000 pays three per cent surtax on the excess over $14,000; that a man whose income is say, $280,000, to take an amount twenty times more, does not pay twenty times as high a rate of income tax but his rate is only three times higher; he pays ten per cent on the excess over $14,000. So I do not think this tax can be said to partake of the characteristics of the "share the wealth" program of the senator south of the line, or that anything drastic is going to happen on account of it.
The Prime Minister in his radio address in Montreal, the one delivered I think on January 9, warned the rich people of this country that they were going to have their patrimony taken from them and that they had better take it philosophically. After seeing this budget they will perhaps not feel so badly. Here is what he said:
Selfish men. and this country is not without them....
This is after he had talked about taxes on income from investments.
Selfish men. and this country is not without them, men whose mounting bank rolls loom larger than your happiness, corporations without souls and without virtue, these, fearful that this government might impinge on what they have grown to regard as their immemorial right of exploitation, will whisper against us. They will call us radicals.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They have put on a special excise tax first of one per cent and then raised to three per cent; a tax on berths and parlour cars; a tax on cable, telegraph and radio messages; a tax on telephone calls; a tax on rubber tubes and tines; a tax on malt products; a tax on unfermented wort; the tax on sugar; a tax on toilet preparations, a tax on toilet soap and a tax on cigarette papers and tubes. Then the tax on corporations has been increased. In 1930-31 it was increased from 8 to 10 per cent. In 1931-32 it was increased from ten to eleven per cent. In 1932-33 it was increased from 11 to 12^ per cent. In 1933-34 it remained the same, and now it is proposed to increase it to 13i and in the case of consolidated returns to 15 per cent. Then there is the new tax of five per cent on non-resident remittances and five per cent on premium payments to residents in Canada. Then there was the increase of the sales tax from one per cent to four per cent and then to six per cent. I have made a summary, Mr. Speaker, and I find that under the brand new taxes of this government which have been imposed there actually has been collected from the people of Canada, up to February 28, 1935, a total of at least 880,000,000. That is on new taxes. Then there is the sales tax, which was increased from one per cent to four per cent, and again to six per cent. The increases of sales tax have cost the people of Canada in the neighbourhood of $180,000,000. From the increases in the income tax on corporations the government have collected $37,300,000. In other words, the total of new taxes, together with the increased sales tax and increased corporation income tax, is about $298,000,000, or in round figures S300,000,000. And that figure is probably a very modest estimate. But in addition there has been an increase in the individual income tax. The exemption stood at S3,000 when this government came into power. That exemption was twice reduced, first to $2,400 and then to $2,000, so as to hit the man with the small income, and the twenty per cent discount was removed. The exemption for children also was reduced from $500 to $400. In 1933 there was the change in the first bracket, increasing the tax from two per cent to three per cent, and the increase continued all the way up. There was an additional income tax on all incomes over $5,000. There is no possible way by which I could figure out the total increase put on the backs of the income tax payer by all these changes, but I think the estimate I have given regarding the new and increased taxes other than the personal income tax

is well within the mark, namely that they have resulted in over $300,000,000 more being collected from the people of Canada during the life of this government than would have been collected if taxes had remained as they were when this government took over.
So I come to sum up the financial record of the government during the past five years because after all, as I said, this is their farewell budget. During the past five years Canada has dropped in world trade from fifth to eighth place. My hon. friends can give all the world statistics they like; that is the situation. Canada, one of the countries away up in total world trade, has dropped from fifth to eighth place; that gives the Minister of Trade and Commerce the comparison he asked for. Then, during the past five years her average total trade has been $1,200,000,000, or only one-half the average total trade during the previous five years. In the next place, under the previous five years of Liberal administration there were surpluses on ordinary account totalling $413,000,000, though taxes had been reduced by an estimated total of $180,000,000. Compare this with the five years of Conservative administration when there have been deficits on ordinary account totalling $157,000,000, though new and increased taxes have brought in over $300,000,000 without taking into account the heavy increases in personal income tax. In the five years of Liberal administration the debt was reduced $257,000,000, while under the present government the debt increase has already amounted to $812,000,000, and we are facing a deficit of probably $125,000,000 to $150,000,000 next year. Lastly, in spite of all the promises of 1930 there are over 1.200,000 people on relief in Canada at the present time.
My hon. friends say, " Oh, well, but you are not taking account of the depression." Canada was in the best position of any country in the world to ride through the depression. Canada was a country that sold the necessities of life. People had to eat; people had to live, and Canada was a country which provided the things they needed. Yet our trade has been crippled and strangled. This government has had all the power of parliament, it has had a majority which could put through any legislation it required; it has had the full resources of the treasury in the form of a blank cheque forced from parliament, and it has had and has made full use of the most autocratic and dictatorial power. They have had their own way absolutely in trying out their policies and at the end of five years this is the record as I have just given it.
Sensing their danger, as a result of the byelections they put on a most remarkable

Railway Act

Rates on Grain
profession of repentance and announce a program of reform. The details are withheld, but are to be given to parliament. The details are now disclosed, and we find a series of measures which prove to be only a hollow echo of the flow of fulsome rhetoric with which they were announced, and the principles of which are altogether foreign to the policies previously espoused by this government. This budget, in its expression of sudden concern in regard to external trade, is just a part of that same weird change which has taken place in government thinking since the by-elections of last September. What this government cannot seem to realize is that the sincerity of all these new professions is being tested in the country by the recollection of the solemn pledges of 1930. And they are only fooling themselves if they believe that these last minute recantations are going to make Canadians forget. There is no escaping the issue; and we on this side of the house believe we express the views of the great mass of the citizens of this country when we say that what the people of the dominion are waiting and anxious for is a chance to register at the polls their opinion regarding the record of this government in the past five years and the grotesque attempt it has made to obscure that record by these eleventh hour professions. The results in nine by-elections and four provincial elections from the Atlantic to the Pacific leave no room for doubt regarding the temper of the electors. We call upon the government to finish the business of the session, to dissolve parliament, to let the people speak at the polls and to make way for an administration fresh from the electorate with a mandate to undertake the task of repair and reconstruction on principles of Liberal economics and Liberal ideas. Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, I beg to move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie):
That all the words after the word "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
This house regrets that the proposals submitted by the Minister of Finance on March 22 are entirely inadequate to meet the serious and acute situation prevailing in Canada and afford an additional reason why appeal to the people should not be longer delayed.

speechtext:
Bill No. 27, respecting Canadian Marconi Company.-Mr. Sullivan.
Bill No. 43, for the relief of Clarence MacGregor Roberts.-Mr. Bell (St. Antoine).
The house resumed from Friday, March 22, consideration of the motion of Mr. Reid for the second reading of Bill No. 38, to amend the Railway Act (rates on grain).

Mr. Speaker, when nine o'clock was called the other evening I was replying to some of the arguments advanced by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion), and this evening I propose to deal with them at further length. The minister has commended me upon my persistence in bringing this matter before the house, and it has been said that this question has been the subject of debate for many years. I would point out that the Railway Act amendments were passed in 1925 but the question was not presented in form of a bill until 1931. As I said at that time, and as I repeat now, I believe that the House of Commons is the place to settle this particular question, and before I finish I shall endeavour to prove this contention.
In my previous remarks I stated that the rates to the east were considerably less than those to British Columbia, and the other evening the minister replied by stating that the rates to the east were largely paper rates. I have before me some information which I should like to put on record in connection with the grain movement through eastern and Pacific ports. I have the figures from the year 1929 but I shall only give those for last year. Over 6,000.000 bushels of grain passed through the port of Saint John. The grain movement to Halifax totalled 2,301,937 bushels, while 49,788,385 bushels passed through the port of Montreal. I want these figures to be on record because I am contending that the greatest revenue derived by the railway companies is that derived from the handling of grain through Pacific coast ports.

I am sure the hon. gentleman has no desire to be unfair and he must
Railway Act-Rates on Grain

admit that practically all of that grain would
be carried water and rail. I said that the rail rate from the head of the lakes to Montreal was largely a paper rate.

I admit that I am not quite
sure but I would be inclined to believe that the grain shipped from Halifax and Saint John had been shipped during the winter months.

That may be correct but
it would have reached Montreal by water and rail.

Perhaps we can agree to differ on that. I still contend that the rate set by the railway companies was more than a paper rate; it was intended that business would be done with those rates. This argument has been used quite often by the railway companies -when they appeared before the board of railway commissioners but I still claim that it is an actual rate.
The railways derived their greatest benefit from the carriage of grain to British Columbia as over 100,000,000 bushels of grain passed through the Pacific ports last year. A large portion of this grain went to the old country via the Panama canal. Compare this to the total movement of only 83.000.000 bushels through Montreal, Saint John, Halifax and all other ports on the eastern Atlantic. If I had the time I could place on record figures which would show that there 'would be a greater return to the railway companies if more encouragement was given to the shipment of grain via the Pacific coast. Although there is a handicap of S9.000 per ship as a toll through the Panama canal, more grain left the Pacific ports for the old country than was shipped out of the eastern ports. I do not think these figures can be refuted.
Tb" other evening the minister disputed the statement I had made that the export rates to Vancouver or New Westminster were not on a par with and were in fact higher than the export rates to Fort William. It was not my intention to deal with export rates at any length but I think I should attempt to prove my contention that the export rate to Vancouver is higher than the export rate to Fort William. In order that the house may more easily understand my figures I have reduced them to net ton miles. I shall first take the Canadian Pacific railway, over which the distance from Calgary to Vancouver is 642 miles. The export rate is 20 cents per hundred pounds, and if one reduces that to ton miles it means -6 cents per ton mile, so that the railway is carrying grain for export through the ports of New Westminster and Vancouver at the rate of

60 cents per ton for every hundred miles. Coming to the Calgary-Fort William stretch, the distance is 1,243 miles. The rate is 26 cents per hundred pounds for export and 26 cents for domestic. The 26 cents works out at -3 cents per ton mile and for 100 miles per ton the rate is 30 cents-just one-half. Yet the minister rose in his place to contend that we were on a level with the rates to Fort William. I want to put on record another comparison-Red	Jacket to Fort
William, which is under the Crowsnest pass rate. The distance is 646 miles, four miles greater than from Calgary to Vancouver, and the rate there is 18 cents per hundred pounds. How can the minister say that the rates for export through the Pacific coast ports are equal, or that we are enjoying Crowsnest pass rates? I dispute that statement. I do not want to be drawn into a controversy over export rates; that can come up later. I want to develop the argument that we in British Columbia are being soaked in connection with the grain requirements we use in that province. The minister made the statement that at the present time the railways are having financial difficulties and that this would not be the proper time for a change inasmuch as it would mean a loss in revenue. Let us see what they are doing as regards passengers, and compare that with the freight business. I suppose he would argue that this is not the proper time to reduce passenger fares.
No; I agree with my hon. friend in that regard.
Yes, but he stops at passenger fares. He takes the view that it is all right to induce passengers to travel, but when it comes to encouraging freight, oh no.
The reason is that passengers are all being carried by motor busses and we want to have passengers on the railways.

Well, if no change is made in freight rates a great part of the traffic in this country will ultimately be carried by trucks. Last year I pointed out how many trucks had hauled apples from Okanagan to Vancouver. I showed also the traffic that was being carried by the railways before the trucks began to be used extensively. The trucks have entered into competition with the railways and no effort is being made by the railways to encourage that traffic. Even before 1925 every appeal that was made to the board of railway commissioners or to the railways themselves met with the argument now advanced by the Minister of Railways, that it would

Railway Act-Rates on Grain
never pay them to lower the rates. They used that argument when times were good, and as a matter of fact it is their stock argument: This is not the time to do it. The fact is that no time has been the right time so far as the railways are concerned; no time has been the right time from the point of view also of the Hoard of railway commissioners, and I suppose that no time will ever be the right time until parliament takes upon itself the task of compelling them to take the necessary action. Lower rates, I maintain would mean greater returns to the railways in consequence of increased traffic.
I am surprised at the attitude which labour has sometimes taken in this regard. Some of them seem to think that if freights were reduced it might result in the dismissal of some employees, and therefore some sections of labour have been rather opposed to the reduction of freight rates. I would point out to labour however that any time a reduction has taken place an increase in traffic has generally followed, with the result that more employees have been engaged. I do not believe therefore that there is any danger from that point of view, and past experience leads me to make that assertion. I have placed one or two figures on the record to show that the rates in the United States for coarse grains were lower than we in British Columbia have paid.

I know that my hon.
friend does not wish to misrepresent the situation. I have checked up these figures since, however, and I have statements from the board indicating that the hon. gentleman is wrong. He quoted, in regard to low grade grains in the United States, a statement which he held in his hand the other night-I think it is the same statement I have here-which shows that the domestic rates went out of operation about six months ago. They are not in force at the present time. I wished to correct my hon. friend before the evening was over, and I should like him to deal with that aspect of the matter if he will.

I will deal with that. Coarse
grains are carried from Cut Bank, Montana, a distance of 732 miles, at the rate of 38i cents per hundred pounds. How does that compare with ili cents for a distance of 642 miles to Vancouver and New Westminster? Is that a higher rate or a lower? I maintain it is a lower rate. The railways of the United States are carrying flour and coarse grains 732 miles for 38J cents under the new rate as compared with 4H cents for a distance of 642 miles, as paid by us in British Columbia.

But those were not the
figures the hon. gentleman gave the other night.
I gave 34i cents.
Which was wrong.

I still maintain that the rates there are lower. The minister may change the figures if he will, and I will take him up on any figure he likes to quote. From Billings, Montana, to Seattle, a distance of 1,012 miles, they are carrying coarse grains for 40^ cents per hundred pounds, carrying it at the rate of one cent per hundred pounds less, and for a distance of 1,012 miles as against 642 to Pacific ports.
But we are carrying feed grains for 30 cents, 10 cents less.
We were glad to get that small reduction, but may I point out that that is a temporary rate.
I do not think so.

Well, when it was introduced
in parliament it was stated by the minister that the agreement would last one year and at the end of one year it was said the rate would continue a little longer. If that is not temporary, what is it?

It has been in force two
years.

But it may be discontinued at
any time. At any rate it is only a sop handed out to keep us quiet. There is another aspect of this matter which I want to touch upon, something that is very important and that the minister has not discussed. While they are carrying coarse grains into the state of Washington, a greater distance and for less, they are also carrying produce from Washington state to the Atlantic; and are carrying eggs and butter at cheaper rates back to Chicago and New York than the rate charged us from British Columbia. So that both ways the railways in the United States are carrying coarse grains at a cheaper rate, and are besides carrying the produce of the American farmers into the eastern markets at a far lower rate than we in British Columbia are charged in connection with our produce.
I maintain that the attitude of the Canadian Pacific Railway has been one of obstruction so far as British Columbia's effort for redress is concerned. I would point out to the minister that the Canadian Pacific Railway, the dominant railway in this country, has taken an attitude of hostility to British Columbia. In carrying grain to the Pacific
Railway Act-Rates on Grain

coast the Canadian Pacific Railway have an advantage first of all of 132 miles over the mileage of the Canadian National railway, and in addition they receive $3.50 for every car of grain that goes by the Canadian National to the coast. The Canadian National is therefore penalized a total of $8.75 per car on all grain that goes into the city of Vancouver, and of that amount the Canadian Pacific take $3.50, so that they have the advantage over their competitor by that sum and they also benefit by the fact that the mileage from Calgary to Vancouver is 132 miles less, which is a very considerable advantage, because that distance, I believe, means the services of more than a day's train crew. I understand a crew runs about a hundred miles a day.
As regards the people in central Canada, the population from the great lakes east in Ontario and Quebec get their feed and flour requirements carried there at half the cost that we do in British Columbia, with the result that the eastern farmers, those who go in for stock raising and so on, are able to obtain their bran and shorts and mill feed requirements much cheaper than we can do in British Columbia, although they are further removed from the wheat fields than are the people of our province. Thev are able to get that advantage ovring to the fact that when grain leaves for the east, there is no such thing as a domestic rate: the grain is designated simply as grain; but when it leaves for western points the railways designate it as either for export or domestic, although both kinds of grain are carried alongside each other by the same train crews over the same route and at the same time.
As regards the board of railway commissioners I do not know w'hether it was the fault of there not being a chairman that we lost the appeal last fall; but when one looks over the evidence one can realize-and I say this in a kindly spirit-that we could hope for little from the acting chairman, because ever since he has been a member of the board his decisions have been against appeals made by British 'Columbia. After consideration, in my opinion the board of railway commissioners have never protected the western provinces.
Might I point this out for the benefit of the house: British Columbia is paying much higher rates not only for her grain requirements but for all products shipped to the east, and I am surprised that the east has not given that province support in her fight for equality, because British Columbia has I believe dealt very kindly with the reanu-
[Mr. Reid.l
facturers in the east. In 1933 it is estimated that British Columbia bought from eastern Canada a total of $81,000,000 worth of goods, and all eastern Canada bought from that province in that year was $4,500,000 worth, so that the advantage is all in favour of the east.
The minister in his remarks-and I was very sorry to hear him make this statement- almost threatened the Liberals. He said: "The government is going to turn down this bill and I warn the Liberals that thev had better be very careful before they get into power, if they do so, how they vote on this bill." He also took a little time to put on the record how many appeals had been made to the board of railway commissioners, and he said that out of forty-eight appeals only some three had been allowed. He was telling us in plain language: You people from British Columbia might just as well quit fighting for your rights; parliament is not going to do anything for you; you need not go ,.o the board, nor need you appeal to the governor in council, because since 1904 the governor in council has only dealt with three appeals out of forty-nine. Is it any wonder that in that province you hear some people saying we should secede from the east? I am not advocating that we should do so; far be it from me, but it is little wonder that the minds of the people are turning toward secession when they realize the treatment they have been receiving for many long years. And might I point out if British Columbia had her own customs and excise, something she had before confederation, she would not be as badly off as she is to-day; she could probably then take care of the freight rates, or at least the burden would be a little easier on her people.

I do not like interrupting, but as the hon. member knows I have no privilege of reply because he is closing the debate, and I know he does not desire to give the record wrongly in any detail. I mentioned one in an interjection I made a few minutes ago. The other evening he stated that from Montreal to Ottawa the old Canadian Northern cost $187,000 a mile. My question is: Did he not include in that-and I believe he did-the cost of the Mount Royal tunnel of $13,000,000? I am informed that he did, and I should be glad to have him deal with the matter.

As to that I am not at ail sure, but the record from which I obtained the information and which I have under my hand gives no account of the Montreal tunnel.

Railway Act-Rates on Grain
This came up in evidence before the board of railway commissioners and Commissioner Oliver is the authority I quote.
I believe the hon. gentleman is correct about that. I am informed that it did include the Mount Royal tunnel.
Even if it did, why should it not? Was it not a cost? That does not detract at all from my argument.
Except as speaking of one particular section with the very high cost of a tunnel added to it.
I have not added the cost of the Quebec bridge, which cost $30,000,000; that would be a higher cost per mile.
The hon. gentleman objected to my adding in the mountains, so I was just wondering.

Neither the minister nor any other person, I say in all kindliness, has ever been able to disprove the statement that it cost less to construct the railways into British Columbia; the construction, maintenance and operation costs in the east were higher. If I had time I would be able to show that the grades into Fort William are steeper than the steepest in British Columbia. I was rather surprised to realize this; I looked them up again only to-night. However I see my time is going on, but whenever the minister wants to stage a debate on this, why that is all right with me.
The hon. gentleman's time has expired.
May I be permitted with the consent of the house to suggest that the hon. gentleman be allowed to go on for about ten minutes more-
Five minutes more.
-five minutes more, because I did interrupt him a number of times.
Carried.

I will come down now to my final appeal, and I thank the house for allowing me the extra time. The minister might review very carefully both lines of railway. We are to-day looking for a solution of our railroad problem, and in looking over the roads I have come to the conclusion that so far as British Columbia is concerned the Canadian National could probably be used more and to better advantage for the hauling of freight at least than could the Canadian Pacific. The Canadian National is a more recently built railroad and it has the finest and best grades in Canada. When one considers that the same type and weight of engine can take fifty cars of grain by the Canadian National as against eighteen to twenty cars by the Canadian Pacific, I think my suggestion is very obvious. One must not lose sight of the fact that only sixteen per cent of the Canadian Pacific is main line-I refer to the prairies-and over eighty-four per cent are branch or secondary lines, which are more costly in operation.
I will close by making a final appeal to the house. Apparently the board of railway commissioners have told us that owing to past judgments we need not come before them any more, that the case is finally disposed of. I have an appeal before the governor in council, which is slightly different from what is sought by my bill. It asks that rates on feed grain and mill feeds be reduced to the level of export rates. This bill asks that the Crowsnest rates apply to all grain and grain products coming into British Columbia for domestic purposes. Surely I have a right to come to the court of last resort. I am not bringing into the house the general question of freight rates. Even in 1925 the government did not object very strongly to the bill on the Crowsnest pass rates; they said "carried on division." They were careful not to register a vote against the Crowsnest rates being put into effect. We are asking only for the same consideration on feed grains and mill feeds as this parliament by statute in 1897 and again in 1925 gave to the east and the maritime provinces. I am appealing for support from all members including the eastern members. I have no fault to find with the members from the maritimes; they have a case of their own, but might I point out to them that, leaving aside the fact that they get between six and seven million dollars returned to them by way of subsidy, their schedule rates are lower than in British Columbia. Surely they can join with us at this time and give us the justice that we have been seeking to obtain for the last twenty or thirty years.

If I may ask the hon.
gentleman a question, as one who has represented the provincial government in this case before the board of railway commissioners, do I understand him to say that the appeal has been carried to and is now before the governor in council?

I said that the appeal before
the governor in council was a little different from the present bill. The appeal I made to the board of railway commissioners and which is now before the governor in council asks that the rate on feed grains and mill feed
Railway Act-Rates on Grain

be reduced to the export basis. The present bill asks that the Crowsnest pass rates apply on all grain and grain products going to British Columbia for domestic purposes.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to say a few words on the budget I wish first to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) on what I consider was the clearest and most complete statement of the business of the country that Canada has heard for many a day. I wish also to congratulate the Prime Minister of Canada and
The Budget-Mr. Myers

the present government for having so conducted the affairs of Canada during the five difficult years through which we have just passed as to make the delivery of such a budget possible.
I listened with my usual interest to the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) who always acts as the financial critic for our friends on the other side. I have always admired the cleverness of an orator and, may I say that on former occasions the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth has excelled himself as a financial critic. To-day however I felt sorry for him, because at the beginning of his remarks he was attempting to criticize the budget of a government whose actions have met with the approval of the Canadian people. Throughout his observations the hon. member laboured very hard to make the best of a very bad cause, and had it not been for the fact that he is a skilful lawyer and has an exceptional gift of oratory, I do not believe he would have succeeded. Listening to him this afternoon I concluded he was a much better lawyer than politician and a much better politician than Canadian citizen, or he would never have attempted to criticize the budget presented by the Minister of Finance.
Canada has come through four or five very difficult years; these have been trying times not only in our history but in the history of the whole world. It is pleasing to note that notwithstanding the fact the government faced an almost impossible situation when it came into office, both as to finances and as to trade, we now have succeeded on ordinary account to the extent of having a substantial surplus to our credit. It is pleasing also to note that the Minister of Finance has budgeted for a surplus approximating about $21,-
000.000 for the coming year.
Unfortunately problems over which this government or the governments of any country have little or no control must enter into the picture. In Canada we are faced with a railway problem and must decide what we will do with it. It is not necessary nor is it my intention to follow the many figures quoted by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth, -but in passing I should like to say that all hon. members are interested in the Canadian National Railways. We wish all our railways well, and it should be the aim and object of every true Canadian citizen to try in every way to promote the interests of those railways. Especially should this be true so far as the Canadian National is concerned, because the Canadian -people have a direct interest in that system. I believe the railway management as at present constituted

is doing its very best under difficult circumstances. I would go further and state that railway employees throughout the dominion are loyal to the railway system, whether they be connected with the Canadian Pacific Railway or the Canadian National Railways. They are endeavouring to the best of their ability to further the interests of the roads with which they are connected.
We need not look very far to encounter some of the difficulties. Hon. members opposite will say that the high tariff policy of the Conservative party has clogged channels of trade, that we have done this, that and the other thing, and that we have not acted in the interest of the railways. One need only walk down the streets of this city of Ottawa to observe one factor which has had an adverse effect on the development of our railways. The condition, which I shall describe in a moment, is common to every country and at present I can see no way of getting rid of it. As a matter of fact I do not believe the people of Canada would want to get rid of it. I refer to the motor trucks and the large transportation outfits we see in our cities and on our highways. Only to-day I saw on Bank street the largest transport I have ever seen. It had come to Ottawa from the city of Montreal, and is operating in competition with the railways in which we have an interest. I do not know what can be done about it. The figures given by the Minister of Finance would lead us to believe that trade is recovering quickly, and it would seem to me that in years to come the railways may make a -better showing than they are now making. Yet I am not prepared to say, in view of what may be seen abroad in the land to-day, that -our railways will ever be able to make revenues and expenditures balance. We must make up our minds to assist the railway by subsidies, by payment of their deficits or by whatever method may be found necessary.
One fact is certain, namely that we cannot do without railway facilities. The great distances to be overcome, the heavy commodities to be transported, such as wheat from western Canada, coal from the maritimes and Alberta, lumber and farm products from other sections of the country which can be moved only -by railway, lead us to believe that railways are a necessity, and that being so we should do our very best to assist them in every possible way.
Much has been said about the unemployed and unemployment relief. I believe the government has dealt with those problems most generously. All h-on. members regret that a

The Budget-Mr. Myers
portion of our citizens is unemployed, and regret further the fact that many of our people have found it necessary to accept relief. Possibly more are depending on relief than should be depending upon it. However, be that as it may, we must face the problem of unemployment and deal with it as best we can. I repeat that this government has been most generous in the way it has dealt with relief, with the unemployment question and in its treatment of the different provinces and municipalities. 1 noticed in the press of this morning that about eighty mayors of different cities throughout Canada met yesterday in Montreal. There is no reason why mayors of cities should not meet, but we know that sometimes at their meetings they make strange statements and pass stranger resolutions. So far as unemployment relief is concerned they were of the opinion that all they had to do was to pass the responsibility over to the dominion government. They would let the dominion government put up the money and foot the bills of the cities, the municipalities and the provinces. While reading the newspaper article and again while the hon. member for Shefburne-Yarmouth was speaking so eloquently and stating his belief that after the next election the Liberal party would be returned to power, I thought it strange in view of the assurance which he seemed able to give the house that the mayors who met in Montreal yesterday had not postponed their meeting about six months until the right hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), so famous for his generosity as expressed in 1929, came back into power. Then all they would have to do would be to come to him and he would hand out five cent pieces for the whole Dominion of Canada.

The Dominion of Canada, along with the rest of the world, has been facing difficult times, but we have another problem on our hands which has not faced the other countries. I refer to the drought stricken areas in the western provinces, a most unfortunate situation. I had the privilege of going through that country two years ago and I saw what it looked like. As a farmer I am able to realize what it means to a man to go out in the spring of the year with high hope in his heart to put in a crop which he may never reap. I commend this government for every effort put forth on behalf of these people in the western provinces who have been stricken so severely. Not a dollar spent on
their behalf has been wasted, and it is a credit to this country that this problem has been dealt with in such a generous manner.
The hon. member for Shelbume-Yarmouth sought to convey to the house and to the country the impression that the present government has always tried to increase the tariff. To my mind nothing is further from the truth. Ever since this government came into office it has been seeking in every way possible to clear the channels of trade and to lower the tariffs against countries which show an inclination to do the same thing for us. Time will not permit me to go into this matter to any great extent, but figures have been placed on Hansard time and time again in connection with the tariffs of other countries, both at present and for the past five or six years. I could give the tariffs at present prevailing in Germany, in France, in Italy, in Czechoslovakia, in the Argentine, in Ireland and in many other European countries, but these have been given time and time again and no purpose would be served by repeating them. Whatever my opinion may be worth, it is that the tariffs of these countries are at least fifty per cent higher than they should be. There is one fact which I would draw to the attention of hon. gentlemen opposite: these tariffs were raised during the life of the previous government. There is not one single instance that I know of where an increase occurred in the tariff of a foreign country since this government came into office.
We were told by the Minister of Finance that since this government came into office and through the workings of the Ottawa agreements the tariff has been reduced on 250 items while 150 items have been put on the free list. This was done to facilitate the movement of trade and commerce between the different parts of the British empire. A reading of the reports issued by the bureau of statistics or of the newspapers of the country will show an increase in trade and commerce brought about by these agreements.
. A statement was made the other evening which I cannot allow to pass without correction. The debate on the budget is more or less a free for all fight and an hon. member is entitled to bring anything he wishes to the attention of the house. I have not the pleasure of the immediate acquaintance of the hon. member for Laprairie-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis) and I cannot say whether he is in the house this evening, but on March 21 he made the statement that this government had increased the duty on potatoes since coming into office. This statement will be found on page 1951 of Hansard. If there

I took the trouble to find out just what had happened in connection with the duties against potatoes. My information is that prior to May 2, 1930, potatoes which were imported into Canada from the United States were subject to a duty of 35 cents per hundred pounds. That was one of the countervailing duties in the Dunning budget. On May 2, 1930, the United States imposed a duty of 50 cents per hundred pounds against potatoes from Canada and a countervailing duty of the same amount immediately came into effect. Under a tariff change which occurred in the United States on June 18, 1930, the duty was increased to 75 cents per hundred pounds and a similar countervailing duty was immediately put into effect in Canada. After this government came into office and during the short session of 1930 the countervailing duty was repealed and replaced with a straight duty of 75 cents per hundred pounds. This duty was imposed subject to the maintenance by the United States of the same duty against our potatoes. At that time I happened to be in the very thick of this fight, as I was a director of the Prince Edward Island Potato Growers' Association. I should like to quote the president of the association as follows:
The greatest national service the Prince Edward Island Potato Growers' Association rendered was in 1929, when the industry was threatened by a tariff duty on the part of the United States which would have completely lost to Canada the large markets already mentioned had it not been for the prompt and insistent efforts of the Prince Edward Island Potato Growers' Association, backed by the organizations it had built up in New York, New Jersey and the southern states. The association, through these organizations as spokesman, employed an outstanding firm of barristers in Washington, specializing in tariffs, prepared and submitted an intensive brief to the committee on ways and means of the United States House of Representatives, covering years of marketing, and vigorously set forth reasons protesting against any further increase in tariff.
fMr. Myers.]
The association, without the help of any dealers either in this province or any other province of Canada, faced this crisis alone; and at a cost of approximately twenty thousand dollars, five thousand dollars of which was later paid by the provincial Department of Agriculture, were successful in preventing the duty on potatoes from being raised for the 1929 crop; when some time later the tariff was increased, the increase was kept down to 25 cents a hundred pounds.
It was the intention of the Americans at that time to put on a duty of SI per hundred pounds against Canadian potatoes going into that country, and it was only through the efforts of the potato growers' association of Prince Edward Island that the duty, was kept down to 75 cents. There was so much heat over the question in the United States, and the state of Maine fought it so vigorously, that the congressmen from that state refused on that occasion to take their seats in congress until the president assured them that a tariff of 75 cents would be placed against Canadian potatoes. Let me tell the hon. member for Laprairie-Napierville that when next he undertakes to discuss the tariff on potatoes he had better first acquaint himself with the facts which he intends to present to this house.
I understand that I have but twenty minutes left, and I will use the time to my own advantage and that of the province from which I come. Every man can best discuss the things he knows most aboult, and I desire in the short time that remains just to tell this house what we in the maritime provinces think of the late Liberal administration, the treatment we received from them, and also the treatment that has been accorded us as maritimers and, speaking for my own province, as Prince Edward Islanders, during the term of the present government.
Prior to 1926 the maritime provinces, and I believe rightly, considered that they had not been getting fair treatment from the federal government. I am not here to say whether or not the contention was jusitified, though I believe it was. At any rate, the Liberal administration, taking cognizance of these protestations from the maritime provinces, in 1926 appointed a commission to deal with these maritime claims. That body was known as the Duncan commission and was headed by a very clever man in the person of Sir Andrew Rae Duncan, from the old country.
